ALL SEVEN required lenses have now run and every one of them EXECUTED rather than reasoned — against postgres:17.11, against real MinIO at a pinned tag, against the live stack on 127.0.0.1:8080, and against purpose-built instances on their own ports. NINETY-THREE findings: 21 blockers, 33 majors, 39 minors. All 21 blockers land in a step and none is declined; one MAJOR is declined in writing with its reason in the step it belongs to (SAF-MAJ-7, the name-confirmation gate on DELETE /v1/trips/{id}). AND NINETEEN RULINGS HAD NEVER BEEN READ BY ANY REVISION OF THIS PLAN. v7.1 certified a 32-ruling snapshot, DEC-43..DEC-83, at a size and a hash that were already stale when it wrote them; the file holds FIFTY-ONE, DEC-43..DEC-102, and DEC-84 through DEC-102 had zero mentions across all 261 KB. Two of the nineteen move work INTO scope (DEC-86 closes registration, DEC-92 puts a backup in R4), one closes a stated blocker on R2 (DEC-84's fifteen minutes), one is a fix to SHIPPED CODE that R6 and R7 were about to copy four more times (DEC-89), and one corrects two numbers this plan carries wrongly in six places (DEC-102). THE SHAPE THAT CHANGED MOST IS R1's. It was SMALL and it is now the largest step in the plan, because eight of the nine things it does are defects in code that is RUNNING NOW rather than in code this plan writes: a rename that wipes an itinerary, a date the client's only date input cannot send, a write response that destroys the only copy of a live share token, a 200 with a valid ETag and a truncated body, ten concurrent requests that hang with no status at all, and 15,151 of 15,960 log lines reading durationMs:0. Revised 24 August 2026 against HEAD d781d29.
goal: Take the running slice — one traveller, one trip, five routes, eleven tables, 462 legs green and a 76-assertion arc — and finish the API surface the Travel Log client needs: object storage with content-addressed photographs, the media routes, the remaining fifteen entity and share writes, the public share read against an enumerated allowlist, and `make seed` loading the client's own 85,422-byte log file into PostgreSQL — which this build emits back as 99,271 bytes, and the difference is DEC-46's object ids (DEC-102) so that four of the five lists in the read path stop being guarded by nothing. Eight steps. What is deliberately NOT in these eight is named in `next_slice` rather than planned.

premise: CARRIED VERBATIM FROM THE SLICE, and unchanged by it. The server owns the data: PostgreSQL is the record and the phone is a cache. The phone reads the whole log — one conditional GET, 99,271 bytes at fixture scale through THIS build (DEC-102; the 85,422 this document used to carry is the CLIENT's format-1 file, whose assets are 31-32 character bundle paths rather than DEC-46's 64-hex object ids) — before its first frame, exactly as it reads the file today, so `logbookProvider` stays synchronous and no screen grows a loading state. Writes go to the server and wait for it; there are no offline writes and no reconciliation. Photographs live in S3-compatible object storage, uploaded straight to the bucket and read back through short-lived signed URLs, and the log carries an object id and never a URL. When the server is unavailable a write is refused rather than queued. What is not being built: multi-device conflict handling, invites, roles, password reset, email, a rendered share page, server-side preferences, and real photograph capture.

DEC-63's index proof method — EXPLAIN a cascade and assert the plan changes from Seq Scan to Index Scan — CANNOT WORK. RI checks run in C-level triggers over internal SPI plans and never appear in EXPLAIN, not even under ANALYZE. DEC-70 withdrew it and replaced it with a pg_index.indkey catalog leg plus SET enable_seqscan=off. v6 still carries DEC-63's text.

A nil slice must not reach the wire. `"cityIds":null` makes the client throw on the answer to its own write, because trip.g.dart reads (json['cityIds'] as List<dynamic>) with no null branch. Emit normalises; the write path did not, and no leg saw it — the splice leg re-emitted through Emit and repaired it on the way, and the first draft of the replacement leg sent `"cityIds":[]`, which decodes to an empty NON-NIL slice and survived its own mutation. ANY PATH THAT ANSWERS A BARE ENTITY GOES THROUGH AN EmitX FUNCTION. Every route this plan adds that answers one inherits the rule, and every leg about it must OMIT the key rather than send an empty array.
PostgreSQL 15 is a hard floor, enforced by internal/postgres/testdb and stated in the migration header. v6 named no floor.
two_things_v6_and_the_slice_both_got_wro: THE FORMAT VERSION. internal/logbook stamps `"version": 2` and Emit REFUSES any other value; the client's decodeLogbook refuses anything but 1, with exact equality, and quarantines the file. So the document GET /v1/logbook answers today cannot be read by the client it was written for, and X-Logbook-Format: 1 answers 406 because Formats() is [2]. DEC-40 says the bump 'costs nothing today because nothing has shipped against this backend' — true of the backend and false of the client, which has shipped, does not implement DEC-53's negotiation, and has no HTTP path to negotiate over. It blocks nothing in R1-R8 and it blocks the first real client request. It needs a human ruling; see open_rulings[1].

THE SHARE FLAG DEFAULTS. trips.share_photos and trips.share_notes are `NOT NULL DEFAULT false` in the shipped schema. The client's Trip.defaultSharePhotos and Trip.defaultShareNotes are BOTH true; only defaultShareCoordinates is false. VS7 deliberately leaves the three columns out of the upsert so a create takes the schema defaults — which means a trip created through PUT /v1/trips/{id} comes back with sharing OFF where the same trip created on the phone has photos and notes ON. It is not a leak (the schema is the more private of the two) and it is a divergence nobody has looked at, in a table read by H1's three switches and by the public share read. R1 fixes it, and it is why R1 is first.

changelog.v7_1_what_the_lenses_changed: FIVE BLOCKERS, NINE MAJORS, FOURTEEN MINORS, all folded in, none argued away. The three that matter most are CORRECTIONS TO v7.0's OWN PROOFS, and they share a shape worth naming: each was something v7.0 wrote confidently, in detail, with a command or a predicted red beside it. (1) R5's share-reset mutation GOES GREEN — `UPDATE … SET col = DEFAULT` is legal SQL and reaches the default, so the sentence 'a DEFAULT does not reach an UPDATE' is true only of an UPDATE that does not name the column. (2) DEC-70's `enable_seqscan=off` proof PASSES WITH THE INDEX DELETED, and DEC-70's stated reason for withdrawing the EXPLAIN proof is factually wrong — `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` does report constraint triggers by name with timings, which is a BETTER measurement than the ruling permits. (3) The certified hash of the rulings file did not match the file, and the three ids v7.0 then invented were ids the human already owned — with a real consequence, because R5 cited one of them for a privacy-critical reset. TWO BLOCKERS ARE DEFECTS IN THE PLAN'S DESIGN rather than in its proofs: a mandated write strategy that silently unfiles photographs (PD-06) and a row filter stated one level too shallow (PD-07). Both are invisible to every guard v7.0 named, and both were reproduced here rather than accepted. ONE FINDING IS THIS REVISION'S OWN, in neither lens report: the paired CHECK a later reader will reach for instead of ruling DEC-83's Go rule is UNEXECUTABLE, because it aborts D2's keep branch — DEC-66's blocker recurring one layer along, with the same signature.
changelog.v7_2_what_the_seven_lenses_changed: TWENTY-ONE BLOCKERS, THIRTY-THREE MAJORS, THIRTY-NINE MINORS, across seven lenses, all folded in. Every blocker lands in a step; exactly one MAJOR is declined, in writing, in the step it belongs to. The five that changed the plan's SHAPE rather than its detail: (1) DEC-89 IS A FIX TO SHIPPED CODE. `PUT /v1/trips/{id}` is live and answers 200 to T4's rename while destroying the itinerary and both dates — executed, three cities in, name-only PUT, `SELECT count(*) FROM trip_cities` -> 0. The author had already reasoned this out one line above for the three sharing flags and five columns on the same statement got the other answer. R6 and R7 were about to copy it onto `visits` (whose child is ON DELETE SET NULL), onto photo filings, and onto `walks.points`. So R1 stops being the migration step and becomes the wire-contract step. (2) `emit.go` WAS IN NO STEP'S FILE LIST. The definition_of_done carries the rule that every route answering a bare entity goes through an EmitX function and there was nowhere to land it. Measured: bare `Place` marshals `"visits":null` and bare `Walk` marshals `"points":null`, and the client's codecs read both as non-nullable Lists and throw. City and Photo carry no list key and need none — stated so nobody adds two functions that are noise. (3) THE 'FOUR CLIENT SENTENCES' ARE EIGHTEEN. DEC-56, DEC-84 and go-backend-plan-v6.json all say four, and the four that were named omit `delete_sheets.dart:608` — D3's OWN failed-save line, on the sheet where the user types a trip's name to destroy it. Re-derived here with three commands rather than transcribed. It is the fourth instance of the client's own rule 9: recount the whole table, not the row somebody names. (4) THE OPERATIONS AND STORAGE LENSES BOTH FOUND A BELIEF THIS PLAN HELD. R1's `lock_timeout` does not close the stall class — it bounds the migration's WAIT and does nothing for the requests queued behind its pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (ten of them returned no status at all). And R2's own presign leg omits the header the URL requires, so it goes green on `400 AccessDenied` with no digest checked anywhere. Both are the same class as v7.1's three self-corrections: a proof written confidently, in full, that cannot see its own subject. (5) NOTHING CREATED THE BUCKET AND NOTHING BACKED ANYTHING UP. `MakeBucket` 0 hits, `mc mb` 0 hits across 41 mentions of `bucket`; `pg_dump` 0, `backup` 0 across 261 KB of plan — in a plan whose own premise is that PostgreSQL is the record and the phone is a cache, and whose documented acceptance procedure ended by running `docker compose down -v` against the live volume five times over.

NO WRITE OF AN ORDERED CHILD COLLECTION IS A DELETE-THEN-INSERT WHERE A CHILD REFERENCES IT (PD-06). `visits` has `photos_visit_fk ... ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)`, so the mandated strategy silently unfiles photographs. The leg is a NO-OP RE-SEND of an unchanged array, and the standing assertion is `SELECT count(*) FROM photos WHERE place_id IS NOT NULL AND visit_id IS NULL` = 0 — which is 0 in the client's own log too, so any other answer is a state the model has never expressed.

A DANGLING-REFERENCE CHECK IS NOT A FILING CHECK, and the plan says so where both appear. A cascade that CLEARS a reference leaves nothing dangling, so `expectNoDanglingReferences` and `no_dangling_references.sql` answer 0 under PD-06's defect. Every cascade that can SET NULL carries a second assertion about what is still filed.

THE WHOLE-LOG ROUND TRIP THROUGH POSTGRESQL: seed, then GET /v1/logbook, and the emitted document equals the client's own fixture with exactly two substitutions applied — the two asset locators for their two sha256 object ids. DECODE BOTH AND COMPARE THE DECODED VALUES; IT IS NOT A BYTE DIFF, and the concrete reason is in the reference document: the client wrote `"lat":-45.0` and Go emits `"lat":-45`, at `nz-wish-0` / Roys Peak, which accounts for exactly 2 of the 2-byte length difference. The values are equal as float64 and `(json['lat'] as num).toDouble()` reads both. Quoting the case here is what stops somebody 'fixing' the emitter to print `.0` (CF-MIN-15). This is the strongest leg the project can have and it is the one that retires 'the four unimplemented lists have no round trip through storage'.
Visits come back NEWEST FIRST, because the client reads visits.first.at as lastVisited. Asserted against the fixture's own ordering, not against a rule written here.

ABSENT MEANS LEAVE ALONE, ON EVERY WRITE TYPE (DEC-89). Every field on every write struct is a pointer and a nil field is not written, exactly as `share_photos`, `share_notes` and `share_coordinates` already are. THIS IS A FIX TO SHIPPED CODE: `PUT /v1/trips/{id}` answers 200 to `{id, name}` today and leaves `trip_cities` at zero rows with both dates null. Three legs, each written against THE BODY THE CLIENT ACTUALLY SENDS rather than a synthesised whole entity — a name-only trip PUT, a place PUT with `visits` omitted, a walk PUT carrying only `{dismissed:true}`.

A COUNT THAT MUST NOT FALL, AND IT IS THE ONE ASSERTION THE THREE STANDING GUARDS CANNOT MAKE (DEC-89, SAF-MAJ-5). `expectNoDanglingReferences` sees nothing (the reference is gone, not dangling), R6's place-without-occasion query sees nothing (there is no place), and R7's pair-agreement assertion sees a pair that agrees — so a caption-only PUT that unfiles a photograph passes ALL THREE green. `SELECT count(*) FROM photos WHERE place_id IS NOT NULL` is unchanged across every route in R6 and R7 except `refile` (which raises it) and the D1/D2-delete branches (which lower it by a known amount). It is R5's 'assert on the SURVIVING ROW COUNT, never on error/no-error' rule applied to the routes that do NOT destroy rows.

THE BEGIN RESPONSE TELLS THE CLIENT WHICH HEADERS TO REPLAY (DEC-88). `uploadHeaders` is a flat map of exactly the headers the signature covers, values already encoded server-side, and THE LEG THAT KEEPS IT HONEST IS THAT THE MAP'S KEY SET EQUALS THE URL's `X-Amz-SignedHeaders` MINUS `host`. Without it a Flutter client handed only `uploadUrl` gets 400 on every upload forever, with no way to derive a base64 digest from a hex id.

THE BUCKET EXISTS, AND THE PROOF IS A ROUND TRIP RATHER THAN A HEALTHY PROCESS (DEC-98). `MakeBucket` had 0 hits and `mc mb` had 0 hits across 41 mentions of `bucket`; the official image auto-creates nothing (`MINIO_DEFAULT_BUCKETS` is a Bitnami variable) and `/minio/health/ready` answers 200 with zero buckets. `up -d --wait` proving three healthy services is not proving the bucket, so the arc does a PUT and a GET inside it.

A CONTENT ADDRESS IS WRITE-ONCE AT THE BUCKET (DEC-88). `If-None-Match: *` is signed into the PUT: first PUT 200, any second 412 PreconditionFailed with the original bytes intact — which is what stops a self-consistent checksum for different bytes replacing a committed object. THE COMMIT PATH READS 412 AS SUCCESS, and that sentence is in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES, because without it a client retrying after an unacknowledged success reports a failure.

NO NO-TRANSACTION MIGRATION SHIPS WITHOUT A PROOF THAT IT IS RE-RUNNABLE (DEC-99). A test runs every `-- migrate:no-transaction` file TWICE against the same database and requires the second run to be clean. Executed against the real Migrator: a three-statement file that fails at statement 3 reports the real fault once and then reports `relation already exists` on every boot afterwards, forever, under `restart: always`. The failure message carries the version AND the statement text, not just the ordinal.

A REQUEST HAS A BOUND, A STATEMENT HAS A BOUND, AND A DEPENDENCY OUTAGE ANSWERS 503 WITH `Retry-After` (DEC-96). `httpx.Timeout` has zero production call sites today and the app DSN carries no `statement_timeout`; ten concurrent reads behind one ALTER returned no status at all. The health check's `start_period` goes ABOVE `migrateTimeout` — measured, `health=unhealthy` at t=61s while a CORRECT migration was still waiting for its lock and applied at t=98s.

THE READ IS COMPRESSED AND THE RESPONSE IS COMPLETE (DEC-94). `GET /v1/logbook` answers 200 with a valid ETag and a body cut mid-token when body/link-speed exceeds WriteTimeout — reproduced three times at three rates. gzip level 1 takes the fixture's 99,271 bytes to 6,806 in 0.3 ms. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is set, or the next cache in front of this serves compressed bytes to a client that did not ask. COMPRESSION ALONE DOES NOT REMOVE THE CLASS — it moves the threshold 5-15x — so the WriteTimeout ceiling is raised and SAID OUT LOUD.

EVERY 500 EMITS EXACTLY ONE ERROR LINE CARRYING THE requestId AND THE UNDERLYING ERROR (DEC-101), ASSERTED PER HANDLER PACKAGE BY A LEG THAT COUNTS LINES RATHER THAN GREPPING FOR ONE. `auth_handlers.go` does it and R5-R8 write fourteen more handlers with no rule stated. And `durationUs` rather than `durationMs`: 15,151 of 15,960 lines on the live stack read `durationMs:0`, so no latency question is answerable from those logs at all.

THE LOG IS BACKED UP AND THE BACKUP HAS BEEN RESTORED ONCE (DEC-92). `make backup` is a custom-format `pg_dump`, keep 7, and ONE restore rehearsal is recorded in EVIDENCE.md with its output — a backup nobody has restored is not a backup, and this project already holds that standard for everything else. `make slice` runs under its own COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME and refuses the live project unless `SLICE_DESTROY_VOLUME=1`. NO STEP'S ACCEPTANCE CHECK READS `make seed && make check && make slice`, and that is checked by scripts/check-plan.py rather than by reading.

THE EMITTED TRIP CARRIES `shared` (DEC-91), so revocation survives DEC-85's hashing. Derived as `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM share_links WHERE traveller_id=$1 AND trip_id=t.id AND revoked_at IS NULL)`. It leaks no capability and it is what stops an ordinary rename destroying the only copy of a live token and leaving 'Stop sharing' inert. THE LEG IS WRITTEN AGAINST A TRIP THAT HAS A LIVE LINK — the one v7.1 had uses a trip that does not, which is why it passes.

deletions.why: It has no caller in R1-R8. The media sweep is explicitly out of scope for these eight steps (out_of_scope, and next_slice owns it), and Remove exists only to serve it. By this plan's own standard — OE-10 deleted a struct field for being declared and unread — an interface method with no caller is decoration in THREE places at once. It is worse than OE-10's case in one respect and better in none: it is a DESTRUCTIVE method, with no caller and no test, in the package that will hold the only copy of the user's photographs. AND IT WOULD BE SHAPED WRONG. The database lens's own carry-forward note settles that: with DEC-58's four foreign keys at ON DELETE RESTRICT, a single-statement `DELETE FROM media_objects WHERE …` aborts the whole sweep on the first live object, so the sweep's shape is a NOT EXISTS across all four columns and the store method it wants is not knowable until that query exists.
