deletions.what: DEC-70's proof method (b) — `SET enable_seqscan=off` as evidence that an index is used — and the sentence in DEC-70 giving the reason method (a) was withdrawn.
deletions.why: BOTH HALVES ARE WRONG AND THE DATABASE LENS EXECUTED BOTH. (b) is vacuous for every index on `photos`: with seqscan off the planner picks any index leading on `traveller_id` and filters the rest, so `EXPLAIN SELECT 1 FROM photos WHERE traveller_id=$1 AND visit_id='v-old'` answers `Index Scan using photos_asset_idx … Filter: (visit_id = …)` — the WRONG index, before any mutation — and DROPPING `photos_visit_idx` leaves the same green answer. That is precisely the outcome DEC-70 exists to prevent, in the ruling written to prevent it, for the second time. AND THE STATED REASON FOR WITHDRAWING (a) IS FALSE: DEC-70 says RI checks 'NEVER appear in EXPLAIN, not even under ANALYZE'. Executed: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF) DELETE FROM trips …` prints `Trigger for constraint trip_cities_trip_fk: time=0.248 calls=1` and the same for all five cascades, by name, with timings. The CONCLUSION holds — you cannot assert the plan changed, because the plan INSIDE the trigger is not shown — but the reason does not.
deletions.what_else_changes: The catalog leg (a) becomes the sole load-bearing proof, and EVIDENCE.md says so in terms — with the index dropped it answers `photos_visit_fk | covered = f`, which is the only thing that saw the mutation. If (b) is kept at all it must assert the index BY NAME, parsed out of the plan, rather than 'an Index Scan happened'. AND R4 GAINS SOMETHING BETTER THAN WHAT IT LOSES: the constraint-trigger lines are a real, reproducible measurement of which cascades fired and what each cost, which is a stronger EVIDENCE.md entry than the ruling currently permits a worker to write.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: A proof that passes with its subject deleted, and a justification a reader can disprove in one command.

deletions.what: Two of v7.0's own seven decisions: the one capturing the two fixture PNGs, and the one ordering media before the seed.
deletions.why: Both are now HUMAN RULINGS — DEC-77 and DEC-78 — and one of them is already executed in code at `7b47bee`. A plan decision restating a ruling is a second place for the same fact to live, which is this project's named recurring defect and the direct cause of four wrong counts. Deleting them is not a loss of reasoning: the ruling carries it, and the ruling outranks this document. Note that DEC-77 also lands the files at `internal/logbook/testdata/imagery/`, NOT the `internal/media/testdata/` path v7.0 invented for them — so keeping the plan's version would have left a worker creating a second copy.
deletions.what_else_changes: R1 loses the PNG capture from its work and its file list entirely and cites DEC-77 for the fact that it is done; its size drops and its `why_first` is rewritten, because the irreversible thing it was first for has happened. The plan's decision count goes from 7 to 5 before the six new ones are added. open_rulings RULE-02, RULE-04 and RULE-06 close against DEC-77 and DEC-78, and RULE-01 closes against DEC-76.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: Two facts in two documents, one of which is authoritative and one of which is not, differing on a file path.

deletions.what: R2's leg 'the two TTLs are distinct and both come from config'.
deletions.why: It cannot fail in the way that matters. The security lens put it plainly: a handler in R8 that reaches for the PRIVATE TTL where the public one belongs would redden nothing, because the leg compares the two values to each other rather than checking which one each caller uses. DEC-47 makes S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC 'THE HONEST REVOCATION WINDOW' that D3's and H1's copy is written against, so reaching for the wrong one is not a tidiness bug — it is the screen's promise becoming false. This is DEC-28's class: an acceptance check that cannot fail for the right reason. AND AT v7.2 THE RULING ARRIVED THAT ORDERED THIS DELETION AND ITS REPLACEMENT, WHICH v7.1 HAD NOT SEEN: DEC-84 fixes `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC` at fifteen minutes and says in terms 'R2's TTL leg was DELETED at v7.1 for being unfalsifiable; the replacement must assert the PUBLIC path uses the PUBLIC value — a handler reaching for the private one is the defect, and it would have reddened nothing.' So the deletion stands and the replacement is now MANDATED rather than proposed, and it is written out in R2's test_strategy rather than described.
deletions.what_else_changes: Replaced by a leg asserting WHICH TTL each call site uses — the private one for `POST /v1/media/mint`, the public one for the URLs embedded by `GET /l/{token}` — with a mutation swapping them. The config half is kept, because a TTL that is not configurable is DEC-21's tuning question closed by accident.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: A green leg over the one number that decides how long 'Stop sharing' is a lie.

deletions.what: DEF-03 — the deferral of `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on the application role — and R4 work item 8's conditional clause that carried it ('…go on the same line if DEF-03's numbers are settled by then, and stay deferred if they are not').
deletions.why: IT IS DECIDED, SO IT IS NOT DEFERRED. DEC-96 chose the numbers — 15s and 60s — and put them in R1 rather than in R4, with the reason stated plainly: 'a number chosen and written beats a number deferred.' DEF-03's own justification was §6.4's 'nothing here can measure the right value', and that is no longer true: the operations lens measured what the absence costs, which is ten concurrent requests returning curl http=000 with no status, no body and no error, holding pool slots until the lock cleared. A deferral whose trigger has fired and whose number has been ruled is not a deferral; leaving it in the deferred list is how a decided thing gets re-litigated by the next reader who searches for it there.
deletions.what_else_changes: R1 gains the DSN line (search_path, statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout) that R4 item 8 used to carry conditionally, and R4 item 8 is deleted outright. `deferred_decisions` goes from six entries to five before three new ones are added, and the count is re-derived in sequencing.notes rather than decremented. DB-MIN-14's claimed_fix records this as SUPERSEDED rather than fixed, so a FixVerifier grades it against DEC-96 and not against R4.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: A decided number in the list of things nobody has decided.

deletions.what: The phrase 'DEC-56's four sentences' wherever this plan carries it — R1 work item 6, the client-work risk, and the CLIENT-PREREQUISITES outline.
deletions.why: IT IS EIGHTEEN, AND THE FOUR THAT WERE NAMED ARE NOT EVEN THE FOUR THAT EXIST IN THAT SHAPE. Re-derived here with three commands rather than transcribed: sixteen 'could not be saved' sites, two more asserting the same outcome in different words, and D3's revocation promise — nineteen sites, of which `settings_screen.dart:423` writes `preferences.json` and is genuinely unaffected. The omission is a repeat of a named pattern: v4 corrected v3's misattribution of D3's 'stops working' from H1 and did not recount the set, so `delete_sheets.dart:608` — D3's OWN 'so nothing was deleted', on the sheet where the user types a trip's name to destroy it — is in NEITHER earlier list. Keeping the phrase would send a designer to rewrite four sentences and leave fourteen standing, one of which is the most consequential of all of them.
deletions.what_else_changes: PD-16 carries the eighteen in three classes with their line numbers on `wipe/mock-data`, the derivation is in base.measured as M-EIGHTEEN-SENTENCES with the commands, and CLIENT-PREREQUISITES names `settings_screen.dart:423` as EXCLUDED so a designer does not rewrite a sentence that is still true. This is the FOURTH instance of the client's own rule 9 — recount the whole table, not the row somebody names — and the client's CLAUDE.md records the other three.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: A count that is wrong by fourteen, in the one document written for a reader in another repository.

deletions.what: PD-11's sentence that `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` is what goes into the signature, and R2 work item 3's 'THE LENGTH IS SIGNED THE SAME WAY' as a statement about a CEILING.
deletions.why: SigV4 SIGNS AN EXACT HEADER VALUE, so a signed `Content-Length` pins the upload to exactly that many bytes and can never express a ceiling. Executed by the storage lens: signed `Content-Length: 29`, PUT 29,000 bytes -> 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch with the object absent; PUT exactly 29 bytes -> 200. No chunked bypass either — forcing `ContentLength = -1` gives 411 MissingContentLength. A worker who read v7.1 literally and signed `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` would produce a URL that accepts only a file of exactly the maximum size. THE COMPOSITION IS STILL SOUND and that is why this is a deletion of a sentence rather than of a control: refuse to MINT above the cap, then pin the exact declared byteSize, so a minted URL is not an unbounded write.
deletions.what_else_changes: PD-20 replaces the sentence with the two that are both needed and neither of which is true alone, and names the subtler cost the lens found: a size violation surfaces as `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, indistinguishable from a tampered URL, a wrong content-type or a broken signer, so the phone shows the same failure for a photograph one byte off as for a misconfigured server. The genuine bucket-side range mechanism is named and declined: `PostPolicy.SetContentLengthRange` works (measured: err=nil, a URL plus seven form fields) and is a different client contract and a different step.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: A worker signing the maximum and shipping a bucket that accepts one file size.

deletions.what: The claim, in R1's `why_first` and in the operations row of the lens table, that `lock_timeout` on the migration connection closes the database lens's stall finding.
deletions.why: IT BOUNDS THE MIGRATION'S WAIT AND NOTHING ELSE. Executed by the operations lens against a synthetic 0002 of exactly R1's shape: with the ALTER queued behind an open reader, one `GET /v1/logbook` returned curl http=000 at its own 30s limit — no status, no body, no error — and ten concurrent ones all returned 000 after 18.8s with nine backends in active/Lock. `lock_timeout` would not have changed one of those numbers: the requests are queued behind the migration's PENDING ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and nothing in the request path has a deadline at all. This is the same class as v7.1's three self-corrections and it is the fourth: a control named in a plan, with a reason beside it, that does not do the thing the sentence claims.
deletions.what_else_changes: R1 keeps `lock_timeout` — DEC-96 says so in terms, 'it is the third of three and not the whole' — and gains the other two: `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on cmd/api's DSN, and `httpx.Timeout` wired with a REQUEST_TIMEOUT variable, which the middleware has had written and unwired since VS-time with zero production call sites. Plus the 503 branch, because a request that IS bounded still answers 500 when Postgres is gone, and a 500 tells a client not to retry.
deletions.cost_of_keeping: A stall class recorded as closed, in the step that was supposed to close it.

decisions.status: NEW — structural, and it is the fix for a defect that has now fired twice
decisions.title: The plan's own decisions leave the DEC- namespace. They are PD-nn.
decisions.evidence: Executed. `python3 scripts/check-plan.py` at 89fc93f: `FAIL: duplicate ids: ['DEC-79','DEC-80','DEC-81']`, exit 1 — the renumbering that fixed the collision with the rulings file created a collision inside the plan. And the rulings file has grown twice while this plan was being written: 27 rulings when v7.0 read it, 30 when the security lens measured it, 32 now (DEC-43..DEC-83, 41,823 bytes).
decisions.reasoning: v6 shared one namespace between the plan's own decisions and the human's rulings, because the rulings were merged into the plan. They are no longer merged: `docs/rulings-v3-pending.json` is a separate, growing, AUTHORITATIVE file, and this plan is a subordinate document that cites it. Any number this plan picks in DEC- space is a number the human may use tomorrow, so renumbering upward defers the collision rather than removing it — which is exactly what the first correction did, and it collided again within one revision. A distinct prefix removes the class.
decisions.consequence: Seven plan decisions become PD-01..PD-05 plus six new ones; two of v7.0's seven are DELETED outright because rulings now cover them (OE-14). Every citation in this document resolves to either a `PD-` (this plan's own, and revisable here) or a `DEC-` (the human's, and NOT revisable here) — which is a distinction v6 could not express and which is the second thing that went wrong. `scripts/check-plan.py` now READS `docs/rulings-v3-pending.json` and fails on any `DEC-` id this plan claims as its own, so the next collision is caught by the gate rather than by a lens.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.0; AMENDED at v7.1 by ruling DEC-82, and the amendment is the half v7.0 got wrong
decisions.title: The share flag defaults move to the client's in migration 0002 — and 0002 BACKFILLS the rows already written
decisions.evidence: v7.0's half, still true: the schema had three columns `NOT NULL DEFAULT false` against the client's `defaultSharePhotos = true`, `defaultShareNotes = true`, `defaultShareCoordinates = false`, and the upsert names none of the three, so a create took the schema's answer. THE HALF v7.0 MISSED, executed by the database lens: after the two ALTERs, pre-existing rows stay `f|f|f` while every new row reads `t|t|f`, `pg_attrdef` shows the new defaults, and nothing in the table can distinguish 'written before 0002' from 'the user turned sharing off'. v7.0 said 0002 'touches nothing else' and tested only a NEW trip, so the leg it wrote could not see this.
decisions.reasoning: Ruled at DEC-82: those rows carry a default the CLIENT NEVER HAD, so they are wrong data rather than a choice. The alternative — leave them and document it — puts a permanent, undetectable inconsistency in the one table already written, and `trips` is the one table the slice arc writes on every run. The DEFAULT still carries the create case, for v7.0's original reason: naming the columns on INSERT means an ON CONFLICT clause that sets some columns and not others in a statement whose whole point is that it sets everything, which is the shape the next person tidies into overwriting H1's switches.
decisions.consequence: 0002 is two ALTERs plus `UPDATE trips SET share_photos = true, share_notes = true`, with the reasoning in the file. `share_coordinates` is NOT touched — false is correct on both sides. THE DOWN FILE IS NOT AN INVERSE AND MUST SAY SO IN ITS OWN TEXT: putting everything back to false leaves post-0002 rows wrong in the other direction, so the down file reverts the DEFAULTs only and states that the backfilled rows are deliberately left. R4's seed makes this moot for seeded rows — it writes the values from the client document and refuses a non-empty database — so this bites exactly the trips the slice arc already wrote, which is the reason it is cheap and the reason it is not zero. THE LEG v7.0 LACKED: create a trip, apply 0002, read it back.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.0, unchanged
decisions.title: `make seed` is `cmd/seed`, a separate binary, and never a flag on `cmd/api`
decisions.evidence: internal/seed's own doc comment already says it: the command 'takes its DSN as an explicit flag rather than from the environment, so that an ambient DATABASE_URL cannot aim it at a real database by accident'. v6's S12 planned `cmd/api/seed.go`.
decisions.reasoning: A flag on the server binary puts a command that writes a whole database inside the artefact that ships, where the DSN it would use is the one already in the environment. The refusal against a non-empty log is a guard, and a guard inside a production binary is one review away from being made overridable for a good reason.
decisions.consequence: cmd/seed, taking -dsn (required, no default, no environment fallback), -force and -reset. cmd/api's existing import sweep gains a sibling assertion that cmd/api imports nothing from internal/seed. `-sweep-media` is NOT covered by this and stays a flag on cmd/api when it lands: a sweep is an operational command run against the database it is deployed beside, which is the opposite argument.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.0, unchanged
decisions.title: The asset rewrite is one named function with its own legs, and it REFUSES an unmapped locator
decisions.evidence: The census: two distinct locators across 284 photographs, and the three coverAsset columns draw from the same two.
decisions.reasoning: The alternative — a second generated fixture (DEC-52, deleted as OE-8) — makes the transformation invisible, because what you compare against is the output rather than the rule. A named function is a thing a mutation can break. And the refusal is what a substitution silently gives you instead of an error: a fixture that grew a third image would be loaded with its asset unchanged and rejected by a CHECK three layers down, with the message naming a regexp rather than a locator.
decisions.consequence: `logbook.RewriteAssets(doc Document, byLocator map[string]string) (Document, error)`, rewriting FOUR columns — Photo.Asset and the three CoverAssets — because DEC-46 made all four object ids and DEC-58 put a foreign key on all four. Its legs include the negative, and the error names the unmapped locator.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.0; REINFORCED at v7.1, because both lenses found things only a running system shows
decisions.title: Every step that adds a route adds its arc assertion in the SAME COMMIT
decisions.evidence: VS6 shipped two routes green in `go test` and answering 404 in the running container. VS7's real defect (`"cityIds":null`) was found by pointing the binary at a real database, not by any of 71 mutations. AND NOW: the security lens found the share capability in the access log by running `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/l/CAPABILITY7XY` and reading `docker logs` — `{"...","path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY","status":404}` — which no unit test in this repository was ever going to print. The database lens found its blocker by running a DELETE and a re-INSERT against postgres:17.11 and looking at the row afterwards.
decisions.reasoning: agent-graph-spec-V4 §6.7's second half asks for the client's hard-won LESSONS and not only its entities. This is this repository's own, learned three times now: a green suite cannot tell a guard from a decoration, and neither can a document.
decisions.consequence: scripts/slice-arc.sh grows in R3, R5, R6, R7 and R8; 76 assertions today, re-derived per step. The corollary the record already paid for: an ABSENCE assertion in shell is the easiest kind to write so that it cannot fail, so every new absence leg removes its output files before the request and counts a file curl never created as zero. NEW COROLLARY FROM THE SECURITY LENS: an assertion about a LOG is an absence assertion too — `grep -c token` returning 0 passes just as well when the log file is empty, so every log leg asserts a positive control line in the same run.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.0, unchanged (renumbered from a DEC- id that collided with ruling DEC-82)
decisions.title: The Service layer is written for exactly three operations and for nothing else
decisions.evidence: DEC-62 ruled it and named the three: refilePhoto, removePlace, and the media commit flow — and ruled in the same breath that most routes are plain CRUD where a service method forwards to the repository, and that such a file is noise.
decisions.reasoning: Restated because a ruling with a 'most of' in it gets applied uniformly by the next worker looking for symmetry, and because the three named operations land in three DIFFERENT steps (R3, R6, R7), so nobody sees the pattern in one sitting.
decisions.consequence: internal/logbook grows Service methods for exactly `RefilePhoto`, `RemovePlace` and `CommitMedia`. Everything else goes handler->store. Typed sentinel errors map centrally to DEC-12's wire codes. A leg asserts the Service has no methods beyond the three, so a fourth arrives as a decision rather than as drift.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the database lens's first blocker, REPRODUCED INDEPENDENTLY before being adopted
decisions.title: The visits write is upsert-plus-UPWARD-offset. It is never delete-then-insert, and that is the opposite of what four documents said.
decisions.evidence: REPRODUCED HERE, on the live postgres:17 at 127.0.0.1:5434, in a scratch schema mirroring 0001's constraints. A place with two visits and one photograph filed to `v-old`; `DELETE FROM visits WHERE place_id=...` then re-INSERT of the two IDENTICAL rows in one transaction; afterwards `ph-1 | fushimi-inari | (null)`. The dangling-reference check the plan relies on answered **0**, because the reference is GONE rather than dangling. THE FIX WAS EXECUTED TOO: `UPDATE visits SET ordinal = ordinal + 1000 WHERE place_id=$1`, then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT visits_pkey DO UPDATE SET ordinal = EXCLUDED.ordinal, then DELETE the ids absent from the incoming array — ordinals swapped to `v-old 0 / v-new 1` and the photograph still read `ph-1 | fushimi-inari | v-old`. THE DOWNWARD OFFSET FAILS: `ordinal - 1000` gives `ERROR: new row for relation "visits" violates check constraint "visits_ordinal_ck"`. AND ONE MEASUREMENT NEITHER LENS MADE: across all 284 fixture photographs, `place-only: 0, visit-only: 0` — 95 have both set and 189 have neither. So the state this defect produces (place set, occasion NULL) is one the client's model has never expressed.
decisions.reasoning: Four independent instructions pointed at delete-then-insert: 0001's header mandates it in capitals, the shipped `replaceTripCities` is the pattern named as the one to copy, the prior DBA pass wrote 'the same strategy applies and the same proof covers it' about visits specifically, and v7.0's own R6 leg list said 'this is the delete-then-insert reorder'. It is safe on trip_cities, which has no referencing child; visits has one, `photos_visit_fk ... ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)`. A NO-OP RE-SEND OF AN UNCHANGED ARRAY DESTROYS THE FILING, and every guard in v7.0 is blind to it.
decisions.consequence: R6 mandates the upsert form and the upward offset, with the arithmetic in the file. The offset direction is not a preference: downward violates `visits_ordinal_ck CHECK (ordinal >= 0)` and the set-based `SET ordinal = 1 - ordinal` collides on the non-deferrable UNIQUE. The DEFERRABLE alternative was declined for 0001's own stated reason — it moves the 422 to `tx.Commit()`. THE LEG R6 LACKED: re-send an UNCHANGED visits array and assert the photograph's visitId is unchanged. And the general form goes in CLAUDE.md, because it is a class: A CASCADE THAT CLEARS A REFERENCE IS INVISIBLE TO A DANGLING-REFERENCE CHECK, so 'no dangling references' is not the same claim as 'nothing was unfiled'.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the database lens's second blocker
decisions.title: The public envelope has THREE row rules, not one, and the second is nested inside a row the first correctly publishes
decisions.evidence: Measured against the fixture the seed loads. The one trip carrying a shareLinkId is `autumn-crossing` (token `kyoto-9f2a`, sharePhotos true, shareNotes true). Re-counted here rather than carried: `fushimi-inari` holds **28 visits across four trips** — japan-2026 23, kyoto-in-may 3, winter-light 1, autumn-crossing 1 — and **1 of the 27 unshared visits carries a note**. `kibune` (9 visits, 1 shared), `nishiki` (6, 1) and `bukchon` (2, 1) are the same shape. BOTH OF v7.0's NAMED R8 LEGS PASS WHILE THIS LEAKS: `tofuku-ji` is correctly absent as a wishlist place and the other-trip Kyoto places are correctly absent — those are the two shapes the leg looks for, and they exist in the fixture, so the leg goes green.
decisions.reasoning: v7.0 stated the row filter at the `places` level only. A place accumulates visits across trips BY DESIGN — 'places belong to the city; visits belong to the trip' is the model's own sentence — so a place correctly published because it is on the shared trip carries every other trip's visits with it, their dates and their notes. shareNotes=true, so the note filter does not save it. This is v6's V4-B2 one level deeper, and the lesson is the one V4-B2 already taught: a key-set assertion feels complete and is not.
decisions.consequence: docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md states three row rules: places = distinct places having a visit ON THIS TRIP; **visits within a published place = only that place's visits whose trip_id is the shared trip**; photos and walks = trip_id. R8's leg: publish autumn-crossing and assert `fushimi-inari` comes back with exactly ONE visit and no note from another trip. THE VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE IS WORTH STATING because it is what a reader would notice before a leak: the client reads `visits.first.at` as lastVisited, so an unfiltered array makes the public page show 2027-12-06 (winter-light) as the date of a trip that ended 2027-10-02. Indexing is already right — the lens executed the join and it drives off `visits_trip_idx`.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's first blocker
decisions.title: The capability is redacted in ONE function that four call sites go through, not 'in the log'
decisions.evidence: Executed against the running container: `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/l/CAPABILITY7XY` then `docker logs` gives `{"time":"2026-08-24T02:44:06.974Z","level":"INFO","msg":"request","method":"GET","path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY","status":404,...}`. The control in the same run: `GET /v1/logbook?secret=INQUERYSTRING` logs `"path":"/v1/logbook"` with the query absent, so the query-string half works and only the half it covers is wrong. FOUR sites print `r.URL.Path`: middleware.go:177 (AccessLog), :104 (Recover), ratelimit.go:151 (RateLimit), auth_handlers.go:203 (logFailure). The attribute redactor at logging.go:71 decides on the attribute KEY, and the key here is `path`, so it can never fire.
decisions.reasoning: v7.0 wrote 'the path is REDACTED from the log' — singular — and its R8 file list touched neither middleware.go nor ratelimit.go. A worker patching AccessLog alone would believe the requirement discharged with the whole suite green. AccessLog's own doc comment defends the wrong half ('THE QUERY STRING IS NOT LOGGED … a capability lives in the URL') while DEC-10 puts the capability in the PATH. THE RATE LIMITER'S LINE IS THE SHARP ONE: it fires precisely when somebody is enumerating share tokens, so the one line written during an attack is the one recording the capability being attacked.
decisions.consequence: `httpx.LoggedPath(r)` — a sibling of `ClientKey`, rewriting `/l/{anything}` to `/l/[redacted]` — and ALL FOUR sites go through it. R8's file list gains internal/httpx/middleware.go, internal/httpx/ratelimit.go and internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go. One leg per site and A MUTATION PER SITE: a fix applied to AccessLog alone must redden three legs, or the legs are one leg wearing four names. Each log leg asserts a positive control line in the same run, because `grep -c` returning 0 passes against an empty log.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's second blocker and its fourth major, which are one design question
decisions.title: A route's response policy and its rate budget are FIELDS on Route, not a derivation the next route invalidates
decisions.evidence: Two findings, one cause. (a) v7.0 wired DEC-51's capability headers into R3 and builds the capability ROUTE in R8, five steps later, and R8's file list never touches that middleware — while DEC-51's own evidence paragraph names `GET /l/{token}` as THE motivating case. (b) routes.go:17-18 says in terms: 'The day an unauthenticated route arrives that is not a credential attempt, this becomes a sixth field rather than a derivation.' R8's public read IS that day, and v7.0's OE-10 ruled the derivation stays. Measured on the live server: NO response sets Cache-Control at all — `/healthz`, the 401s and `GET /v1/logbook` return Content-Type, X-Request-Id and Date only.
decisions.reasoning: The consequence of (a) is not cosmetic. `/l/{token}` carries no Authorization header, so RFC 9111 §3.5's shared-cache prohibition — the thing silently protecting `GET /v1/logbook` today — does not reach it. A 200 with an ETag and no Cache-Control is heuristically cacheable by any intermediary, and after 'Stop sharing' a cached envelope keeps handing out live media capabilities for as long as it survives, which unbounds the very window DEC-44 shrank to two minutes. The consequence of (b) is an availability coupling nobody chose: the public read would inherit AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN, a CREDENTIAL budget of 10/min, from the same bucket instance as register and sign-in — so one person browsing a shared trip locks everybody out of signing in.
decisions.consequence: `Route` gains `NoStore bool` and `Limit` (which limiter, not a number). The middleware is applied FROM THE TABLE, so a route's policy is declared beside its pattern and a new route cannot inherit a wrong one by silence. R8's legs: `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` present on the 200 from `/l/{token}`, with a mutation dropping each; and the public read's limit is A NUMBER with its own mutation. R3 asserts the same headers on `POST /v1/media/mint`, as DEC-51 also requires. AND THE HONEST SENTENCE R8 MUST CARRY, which ratelimit.go already carries: the public read's limit is unenforceable behind a proxy until ClientKey learns X-Forwarded-For, and Caddy is deferred to next_slice. OE-10 IS RE-EXAMINED AND STANDS: `Mutating` is still read by nothing, and two fields arriving that ARE read is not an argument for keeping a third that is not.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's third blocker
decisions.title: The content-type allowlist is enumerated HERE, the disposition is restored, and nosniff's absence is a comment rather than a gap
decisions.evidence: A three-part chain and v7.0 was missing all three at once. Grep counts over the 147 KB v7.0: `image/jpeg` 0, `heic` 0, `content-disposition` 0, `contentTypeRe` 0 — the step titled 'the content-type allowlist as a schema constraint' deferred the actual list to the worker. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` was correctly STRUCK by V4-SF3, because S3's response-header override set is closed and no presigned GET can produce it. So v7.0 kept the removal of the fallback defence and dropped the primary one. The shipped schema already accepts the payload and says so about itself: 0001:119 is `CHECK (content_type <> '')`, and its own comment at lines 95-101 calls it 'THE WEAKEST CHECK IN THIS FILE' and states that `text/html; <script>` is accepted.
decisions.reasoning: An object stored as text/html is served AS HTML from the bucket origin, at a URL the public share envelope embeds — stored XSS on the storage origin, reachable by anyone holding a share link. DEC-51 states the defence literally: 'THE DEFENCE IS THE DISPOSITION PLUS THE ^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$ ALLOWLIST, and the residual is named: a mislabelled object is downloaded, never rendered.' A list that lives in the worker's head is a list the schema constraint cannot be written against, which is why 0001's placeholder has been waiting since VS4.
decisions.consequence: `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$` written out in R3's step text, in Go for the 422 naming the field AND as a schema IN-list in migration 0003 — both, on DEC-58's precedent. `image/png` and `image/jpeg` are load-bearing beyond the fixture: schema_test.go:62 seeds shared fixtures with `content_type='image/jpeg'`, so omitting it breaks every leg using that helper. `response-content-disposition: attachment` is restored on EVERY presigned GET, with a leg. V4-SF3's nosniff reasoning is carried forward in a comment beside it so the next worker does not re-litigate a settled point. SEPARATELY, AND IT IS A QUESTION RATHER THAN A DECISION: `heic` has no producer anywhere in this system — the client's shutter is inert by decision and DEC-41 seeds two PNGs — so the allowlist could be one character shorter. That is RULE-09; DEC-51 is a ruling and this plan enumerates it as ruled.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's first major; AMENDED at v7.2, and the amendment is a deletion (OE-18)
decisions.title: The LENGTH is signed exactly as the checksum is — and what that pins is the DECLARED SIZE, never a ceiling
decisions.evidence: v7.0's checksum ban is backed by a grep that CAN fail and a real-MinIO 4xx leg; the security lens calls it 'the best-specified thing in plan-v7'. The parallel size requirement has no grep, no MinIO leg, and no number: `content-length` 0 occurrences, `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` 0 occurrences, and 'the bound' is never given a value anywhere in 147 KB. DEC-51 required `content-length` SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT 'so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping'.
decisions.reasoning: What v7.0 substituted — an API-side 422 before signing, plus a HEAD on commit — binds nobody. The 422 happens BEFORE the capability is minted, and the HEAD only refuses to MARK the object committed; the bytes are already in the bucket. Nothing in these eight steps reclaims them, because the sweep is explicitly out of scope. So one legitimately-minted upload URL is an unbounded, unreclaimed write. The asymmetry was invisible from the definition of done, which listed the checksum grep and the byteSize bound in one breath as though one mechanism enforced both.
decisions.consequence: `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` joins internal/config. THE TWO SENTENCES ARE BOTH NEEDED AND NEITHER IS TRUE ALONE (PD-20, OE-18): `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` is an API-side refusal to MINT, taken before the capability exists; and the signature pins the EXACT declared `byteSize`, so a minted URL is not an unbounded write. SigV4 signs an exact header value and cannot express a range — executed: signed 29, PUT 29,000 -> 403 with the object absent; PUT 29 -> 200; chunked -> 411 MissingContentLength. A leg mirroring the checksum one: a PUT of more bytes than were signed is refused BY THE BUCKET and `store.Stat` errors afterwards — 'a refused PUT that still wrote something is the same defect wearing a 4xx' applies unchanged. The definition-of-done grep covers both halves so they fail together.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's second major
decisions.title: Revoked and unknown do the same WORK, and the leg counts calls rather than timing them
decisions.evidence: DEC-10 reads: "'Never existed' and 'revoked' are the SAME 404 WITH THE SAME WORK DONE, so nothing confirms a guessed token was once real." v7.0 carried only 'byte-identical', and its leg compares bodies and headers minus X-Request-Id. `constant-time` appears 0 times in v7.0.
decisions.reasoning: A handler that returns early on 'no row' but, for a REVOKED row, resolves the trip, checks three share flags and mints media URLs is byte-identical on the wire and still a clean timing oracle for 'this token was once real'. That is a REVOCATION oracle, not a guessing one — guessing is bounded by 31^12 ≈ 7.9e17 and is not the concern — and DEC-67's revoke-then-insert history design is exactly what makes it worth attacking. The precedent is already the strongest thing in this codebase: internal/auth/service.go's eagerly-computed dummyHash, whose leg COUNTS Verify calls rather than timing them, because a timing leg is a flake on a loaded machine and a pass on a fast one.
decisions.consequence: R8 selects the row regardless of `revoked_at` and decides afterwards, so the lookup is the only branch. Its leg counts store calls on both paths and asserts they are equal, in the shape internal/auth/service_test.go already has. v7.0's 'answer 410 for a revoked link' mutation stays — it is a good mutation — but it is no longer the only one.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — and it is a conflict between two instructions that both look right
decisions.title: DEC-83's comment CANNOT go in 0001, and the paired CHECK a reader will reach for instead is unexecutable
decisions.evidence: TWO EXECUTIONS, both run here. (1) THE CHECKSUM. `loadMigrations` computes `sha256.Sum256(body)` over the whole file, comments included, and `Migrate` answers `ErrChecksumMismatch` when it moves — so a `--` comment added to 0001 breaks every database that has already applied it, including the one on 127.0.0.1:5434. DEC-83's stated consequence is 'a comment on the two columns in 0001'. (2) THE TEMPTING FIX. `CHECK ((place_id IS NULL) = (visit_id IS NULL))` — the exact shape of `photos_coordinates_paired_ck`, which sits three columns away in the same table — BREAKS D2's KEEP BRANCH OUTRIGHT. Executed on postgres:17 against a scratch schema mirroring 0001: deleting the place gives `ERROR: new row for relation "photos" violates check constraint "photos_filing_paired_ck"`, `DETAIL: Failing row contains (..., ph-1, null, v-old)`, `CONTEXT: SQL statement "UPDATE ONLY "photos" SET "place_id" = NULL ..."` — and the delete aborts, photograph unchanged. Deleting only the visit fails the same way in mirror image. The two SET NULL rules fire as two separate single-column UPDATEs, so the intermediate row is ALWAYS incoherent and any CHECK relating the two columns sees it.
decisions.reasoning: This is DEC-66's blocker recurring one layer along, and PostgreSQL echoes its own generated statement in both cases — the same signature. DEC-83 is MORE right than its own reasoning states: it declined the composite FK because that changes delete behaviour, which is a decision for the app's sheets rather than for a DBA. The cheap CHECK alternative is not a milder version of the same idea; it is unexecutable, and it is sitting in plain sight next to a constraint of identical shape that works.
decisions.consequence: The comment becomes `COMMENT ON COLUMN photos.place_id` / `photos.visit_id` in migration **0003**, which is forward-only and needs no edit to 0001 — and it is BETTER than a `--` comment for a reason that has nothing to do with the checksum: a catalog comment is readable from `\d+` and from any tool a later DBA runs, where a comment in a file nobody re-reads is not. The comment names this as the SECOND integrity rule deliberately left in Go (DEC-02's cross-kind id uniqueness is the first) AND records that the paired CHECK was executed and aborts D2's keep branch, so the next reader does not spend an afternoon rediscovering it. ONE MEASUREMENT SUPPORTS DEC-83 AND ONE COMPLICATES IT: across all 284 fixture photographs, 95 have both columns set and 189 have neither — `place-only: 0, visit-only: 0` — so the invariant is real in the data even though the schema cannot hold it, which is precisely why leaving it in Go needs a comment rather than silence.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — implementing ruling DEC-89, which is a fix to SHIPPED code
decisions.title: R1 stops being the migration step and becomes the step where what already ships is corrected
decisions.evidence: MEASURED BY THE SAFETY LENS against a real build of HEAD 89fc93f, on its own instance: `PUT /v1/trips/autumn` with three cities and both dates -> 200, `trip_cities` reads `kyoto:0 / osaka:1 / seoul:2`; then `PUT /v1/trips/autumn` with body `{"id":"autumn","name":"Autumn crossing, renamed"}` -> **HTTP 200**, response `"cityIds": [], "start": null, "end": null`, and `SELECT count(*) FROM trip_cities` -> **0**. `TripWrite.CityIDs` is a bare `[]string` and `checkCityIDs(nil)` loops zero times, so absence and emptiness are the same value. THE AUTHOR ALREADY REASONED THIS OUT ONE LINE ABOVE, in a comment, for three columns: 'share_photos, share_notes and share_coordinates appear in neither the column list nor the SET clause … naming them in EXCLUDED-form would silently reset a group this route does not own (SF6) on every rename.' Five columns on the same statement got the other answer. AND EIGHT OTHER SHIPPED DEFECTS WERE MEASURED BY THREE MORE LENSES — see entry_state.inherited_unfinished, which lists all nine with the ruling that closes each.
decisions.reasoning: v7.1's R1 was SMALL and first for a reason it had already discharged. What the seven lenses found is that the thing worth doing first is not a migration at all: it is that the running code answers 200 to a rename that destroys an itinerary, refuses the only date string the client can send, splices a null over the only copy of a live share token, truncates a large read while reporting success, and hangs indefinitely behind a lock. EVERY ONE OF THOSE IS ALSO A CONVENTION R6 AND R7 WERE ABOUT TO COPY — DEC-89 names three of the copies and measures each: an empty visits array unfiles 30 photographs at Fushimi alone (95 whole-log) while every count except one stays put; a caption-only PUT that nulls both filing columns passes all three standing guards; and `walks_points_array_ck` does not stop `points='[]'` because an empty array IS an array, and a GPS track is a recording of a day that cannot be retyped. Fixing the contract once, before eleven more write routes are written against it, is the whole of the argument for the order.
decisions.consequence: R1's title, size, why_first, files, work, test_strategy and acceptance check are all rewritten. It is LARGE. It carries: DEC-89's pointer contract with its three legs and the count that must not fall; DEC-90's refusal of a zoneless date plus the two golden inputs no fixture contains; DEC-91's `shared` field; DEC-94's gzip and the WriteTimeout ceiling; DEC-96's three bounds and the 503 branch and the `start_period` raise; DEC-101's log fields; DEC-102's three date scans; migration 0002 with DEC-82's backfill and `lock_timeout`; and docs/CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md. DEC-100 does NOT land here — it is auth, and it goes to R5 with DEC-86, because putting every measured defect in one step is how a step stops being reviewable.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — from the client-fidelity lens's third blocker
decisions.title: `emit.go` gets a file list. EmitPlace in R6, EmitWalk in R7, and City and Photo need none
decisions.evidence: `python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('docs/plan-v7.json'));print([f for s in d['steps'] for f in s['files'] if 'emit' in f.lower()])"` -> `[]`. The definition_of_done carried the rule — 'EVERY ROUTE THAT ANSWERS A BARE ENTITY GOES THROUGH AN EmitX FUNCTION' — and no step had a file to land it in; only `EmitTrip` exists. Measured in `internal/logbook` by a probe test: bare `Place` marshals `{…,"visits":null,…}`; bare `Walk` marshals `{…,"points":null,…}`; bare `City` and bare `Photo` carry no list key; `EmitTrip(zero)` -> `{…,"cityIds":[],…}`. Client codecs: `place.g.dart:33-35` and `photo.g.dart:46-48` read `(json['visits'] as List<dynamic>)` and `(json['points'] as List<dynamic>)` — non-nullable, no null branch, hard throw.
decisions.reasoning: This is the `"cityIds":null` defect that `emit.go`'s own comment records as having cost a defect against the running server, arriving twice more in the two steps that were about to answer a bare `Place` and a bare `Walk`. The rule was written and had nowhere to live, which is a different failure from the rule being wrong and is not one a green suite can see. STATING THE NEGATIVE IS PART OF THE DECISION: City and Photo carry no list field, so there is no nil slice for the marshaller to write as null, and two more EmitX functions added for symmetry would be exactly the 'empty forwarding methods' DEC-62 warns against one layer up.
decisions.consequence: `internal/logbook/emit.go (EDIT — EmitPlace)` joins R6's file list and `(EDIT — EmitWalk)` joins R7's. The AST sweep the definition_of_done promises is written in R6 rather than R8, because R6 is the FIRST step that can violate the rule and a sweep written after five steps of violations is a cleanup rather than a guard. Every leg about it OMITS the list key from the request body rather than sending an empty array — which is the same distinction DEC-89 makes about the request, arriving on the response.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — from the client-fidelity lens's first major; it deletes a count three documents carry (OE-17)
decisions.title: Eighteen client sentences, in three classes, re-derived by command
decisions.evidence: RE-DERIVED HERE ON `wipe/mock-data`, not transcribed. `grep -rn 'could not be saved' lib/src/screens/ | grep -v '///' | wc -l` -> 16. `grep -rn 'your log is unchanged' lib/src/screens/ | grep -v '///' | wc -l` -> 2. `grep -rn 'stops working' lib/src/screens/ | wc -l` -> 1. Nineteen sites across ELEVEN screens — one per writing control, which is the cross-check that the count is right.
decisions.reasoning: DEC-56, DEC-84 and go-backend-plan-v6.json all say four. Every one of the seventeen failure sentences asserts an OUTCOME a network write cannot guarantee, for exactly the reason v6 states. And the omission repeats a pattern the client's own record names: v4 corrected v3's misattribution of D3's 'stops working' from H1 and did not recount the set, so `delete_sheets.dart:608` — D3's own failed-save line, on the sheet where the user types a trip's name out to destroy it — is in neither list.
decisions.consequence: CLIENT-PREREQUISITES carries all eighteen with their line numbers and splits them into three classes. (i) SEVENTEEN THAT ASSERT AN OUTCOME, whose honest replacement is retry-then-refresh over a genuinely unknown interval — tractable because DEC-33 makes every verb idempotent: trip_screen 263; edit_sheets 383, 453, 514, 603; to_file_screen 101, 102; add_city_screen 136 and 164; share_sheet_screen 240; refile_photo_sheet 197; edit_traveller_sheet 190; profile_screen 241; delete_sheets 165, 366, 608; new_trip_screen 164. (ii) ONE THAT PROMISES REVOCATION, delete_sheets 649, written against DEC-84's `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC = 15m` — the honest sentence is that stopping a share stops new links at once and a photograph already loaded may keep working for up to fifteen minutes. (iii) ONE THAT NEEDS NO CHANGE AND IS NAMED AS EXCLUDED: `settings_screen.dart:423`, which is `preferences.json` and genuinely stays local. NAMING THE EXCLUSION IS THE POINT — a list of eighteen with no exclusion sends a designer to rewrite a sentence that is still true. AND A FOURTH SENTENCE JOINS THE REVOCATION CLASS ON THE SAME MECHANISM (SAF-MIN-10): D1's 'Nothing is recoverable — there is no bin' was true of a JSON file on the phone and is false of a server whose sweep has a schedule of nobody.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — from the client-fidelity lens's second major
decisions.title: Twelve error codes, three lanes, and `unsupported_format` in a lane of its own
decisions.evidence: `grep -c 'Code = "' internal/httpx/errors.go` -> 12. The client's entire error model is `Future<bool>` out of `_commit` and one fixed sentence per surface, so twelve codes collapse to one boolean. AND THE BRIEF'S PREMISE ON THIS POINT IS STALE, which the lens checked rather than repeated: there is no `deleted` code — DEC-04 is WITHDRAWN in v3 ('the failure it managed CANNOT OCCUR') and `grep -rn '"deleted"' internal/` returns nothing.
decisions.reasoning: Three of the twelve need behaviour a boolean cannot express. `unauthenticated` means the credential is dead and the answer is the sign-in screen, not 'your log could not be saved'. `unsupported_format` is PERMANENT, so a client that retries it retries forever — which is the retries-forever hazard the brief attributed to a code that does not exist. `invalid_field` is a client bug, where retrying is the wrong answer and the `field` key is the only thing that says which. And `rate_limited` and `timeout` are the two that SHOULD be retried and are today indistinguishable from the rest.
decisions.consequence: CLIENT-PREREQUISITES carries a table of TWELVE ROWS, each answering the two questions the client's own CLAUDE.md demands of every writing control — where the user stands afterwards, and what the screen says. Three lanes: RETRY (`rate_limited`, `timeout`, and a transport failure, which is not a code at all and is the thirteenth row); REPORT (`invalid_body`, `invalid_field`, `conflict`, `payload_too_large`, `not_found`, `forbidden`, `internal`, `upload_incomplete`); RE-AUTHENTICATE (`unauthenticated`). `unsupported_format` IS ITS OWN LANE AND MUST NEVER RETRY. `_commit` returning `bool` cannot carry that, so the type change is named as client work rather than left to be discovered.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — from the safety lens's third minor, and it is the one whose harm is a screen lying to somebody
decisions.title: `LogbookSource` has a server equivalent, and it is four HTTP outcomes
decisions.evidence: `LogbookSource` appears ZERO times across all 261 KB of plan-v7.json. The client's `logbookSourceProvider` distinguishes `fresh`, `restored`, `unreadable` and `unavailable`, FOUR screens read it (S1, U2, T1, U1), and the client's own record states why it must exist: 'an empty log you have not filled and an empty log that used to be full are the same five lists, so no screen can tell them apart from the log alone', and 'a screen whose copy would otherwise tell you to begin has to know whether you already did.'
decisions.reasoning: Once `logbookSeedProvider` is fed by an HTTP read rather than by `openLogbook()`, a failed or empty response produces the same five empty lists and the natural implementation drops the enum. The user whose server is unreachable is then told to begin, about a record that exists and that they cannot see. That is the exact failure the client spent a whole decision preventing, arriving from the other side — and the server already has the signal: R4 sets `logbook_version` to 1 after seeding precisely because 'a traveller at 0 is served 200 with no ETag by design, which is correct for a log nobody has written'.
decisions.consequence: CLIENT-PREREQUISITES carries the mapping explicitly: 200 with content -> `restored`; 200 with an empty log and a version of 0 -> `fresh`; a decode or format failure (including the 406 on `X-Logbook-Format`) -> `unreadable`; a transport failure -> `unavailable`. IT ALSO SAYS WHAT RETIRES: the client's `logbook_store.dart` becomes a CACHE rather than a record, which retires the quarantine, the sidecar, S1's notice and U2's sidecar export line — and v6 correctly calls that 'a simplification AVAILABLE to the client, not required', so it is carried as availability rather than as a task.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — from the storage lens's first blocker and its first minor, which are one leg
decisions.title: R2's presign legs replay the signed header, assert the S3 error CODE, and carry a positive control
decisions.evidence: MEASURED against MinIO RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z. The plan's verbatim test code builds the PUT with `http.NewRequestWithContext(...)` and sets NO headers. With `x-amz-checksum-sha256` signed and the header omitted, MinIO answers 400 `AccessDenied` ('There were headers present in the request which were not signed') for LYING bytes AND for HONEST bytes alike, and the leg's only assertion is `resp.StatusCode < 400`. So it is GREEN with zero digest verification happening anywhere. FOUR DISTINCT FAILURE MODES LAND IN THAT STATUS CLASS AND ONLY THE LAST IS THE CONTROL: `AccessDenied` (header not replayed), `InvalidArgument` (the hex-instead-of-base64 mistake), `SignatureDoesNotMatch` (wrong signed-header set), and `XAmzContentChecksumMismatch` (the actual thing). Contrast, header replayed with lying bytes: 400 XAmzContentChecksumMismatch. Contrast, `PresignedPutObject` with lying bytes: **200**, object stored.
decisions.reasoning: The step's own stated intermediate red still works — `PresignedPutObject` plus lying bytes really does return 200 — so the mutation proof passes while the green state proves only that SOME signed header is required. That is v7.1's three self-corrections again, and it is the sharpest instance yet, because this is the leg the whole of R2 exists for and it was written out in full with its reasoning beside it.
decisions.consequence: Every presign leg in R2 does three things it did not: replays the header (`req.Header.Set("x-amz-checksum-sha256", base64Digest)` and the same for Content-Type and If-None-Match under DEC-87 and DEC-88); asserts the S3 error CODE parsed out of the XML rather than a status class; and carries a POSITIVE CONTROL in the same function — honest bytes plus the same headers -> 200, and the object present at the expected size. Without both halves the leg is satisfied by a server that refuses everything, which is the vacuous-negative shape v6 already named for the committed-asset validator.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — from the storage lens's third blocker; it replaces a sentence deleted as OE-18
decisions.title: MEDIA_MAX_BYTES is a refusal to MINT; the signature pins the DECLARED size. Both sentences, neither alone
decisions.evidence: Executed: signed `Content-Length: 29`, PUT 29,000 bytes -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`, object absent; PUT exactly 29 bytes -> `200`; forcing `ContentLength = -1` (chunked) -> `411 MissingContentLength`, object absent. The only true range mechanism is a different upload shape: minio-go v7.3.0's `PostPolicy.SetContentLengthRange(1,1024)` returns err=nil and `PresignedPostPolicy` yields a URL plus seven form fields.
decisions.reasoning: SigV4 signs an exact header VALUE. So the bucket enforces `== byteSize` and can never enforce `<= MEDIA_MAX_BYTES`, and the cap remains an API-side 422 taken BEFORE the mint — which is precisely what PD-11 dismissed as 'the API hoping'. The composition is still sound; the prose was not, and a worker reading it literally ships a URL that accepts one file size.
decisions.consequence: R2 item 3 says both sentences. AND IT NAMES THE SUBTLER COST, because it reaches the phone: a size violation surfaces as `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, indistinguishable from a tampered URL, a wrong content-type or a broken signer — so the user sees the same failure for a photograph one byte off as for a misconfigured server. The presigned-POST alternative is named and declined here rather than left implicit: it is a different client contract and a different step, and DEC-88's `uploadHeaders` is what makes the presigned-PUT contract survivable.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — implementing ruling DEC-93, which names 'a few hundred' and leaves the number to this plan
decisions.title: `Walk.points` is capped at 500, in ValidateWalk, with its own 422 naming the field
decisions.evidence: MEASURED BY THE PERFORMANCE LENS, and THE FIXTURE COULD NOT HAVE ANSWERED IT: the sample log's two walks carry SEVEN POINTS BETWEEN THEM, so every size argument in v7.0 and v7.1 was calibrated on a log with no real track in it. Marshalled through the shipped types: 100 points 5,226 B; 1,000 points 51,004 B; 3,600 points 183,277 B; 21,600 points 1,099,390 B — OVER the 1 MiB body ceiling, which is a six-hour walk at 1 Hz. At whole-log scale it is worse: same photograph count, 10x scale, the fixture's 3-4 point walks read in 12.54 ms / 991,675 B against 37.09 ms / 2,821,305 B for 1,800-point walks. And points COMPRESS BADLY — 4.4-6.2x against 15.6-17.5x for the rest of the document — because they are arrays of distinct floats.
decisions.reasoning: 500 is chosen inside DEC-93's 'a few hundred' and the derivation is written rather than the number alone: at the lens's own measured 51,004 bytes per 1,000 points, 500 is roughly 25.5 kB, two orders of magnitude inside the 1 MiB ceiling; and a six-hour walk decimated to 500 fixes is one every 43 seconds, which C2 draws as a polyline and does not need every fix for. IT IS PROVISIONAL AND SAID TO BE, in the same tier as the Argon2 parameters and DefaultSessionTTL: asserted as a value so it cannot move unnoticed, with nothing claiming it is the right value.
decisions.consequence: `ValidateWalk` refuses over 500 with a 422 NAMING THE FIELD — not `http.MaxBytesReader`, which answers `ErrBodyTooLarge` with no field name, so the user's longest walk would fail with a sentence about bytes. Migration 0003 gains the lower bound too (`CHECK (jsonb_array_length(points) > 0)`), because DEC-89's contract makes `points: []` expressible and a zero-point walk is not a thing this model expresses — both fixture walks carry points, checked. AND THREE QUESTIONS CLOSE WITH IT, which is why DEC-93 is worth reading beside DEC-94: the walk write fits the body ceiling with room to spare; DEC-31's whole-log read stays small, so the trigger for per-resource ETags stays far away; and a track stays IN the log document rather than becoming a media object. THE CLIENT'S OWN DECIMATION IS A CLIENT-PREREQUISITES ITEM — the server refusing an over-long track is not the same as the phone knowing to shorten one.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.2 — and it is the plan's ONLY DECLINED lens major, declined along the branch the lens itself offers
decisions.title: DELETE /v1/trips/{id} does NOT require the trip's name in the body, and R5 says why in its own text
decisions.evidence: The finding is real and is stated fairly: D3 is the most guarded control in the client — it itemises four consequences beside the words 'deleted' and 'kept' and then makes the user TYPE THE TRIP'S NAME before the action arms — and the API behind it requires a bearer token and nothing else. R5's work item reads 'implements D3's own table exactly and nothing more', and 'nothing more' turns out to include the gate.
decisions.reasoning: THE LENS OFFERS TWO BRANCHES AND THIS PLAN TAKES THE SECOND, WHICH IT NAMES: 'If that is judged over-strict for a single-user loopback stack, then say so IN R5 with the reason.' Three reasons, in order of weight. (1) The gate the sheet has is a gate on the HUMAN, and its value is the pause before the typing; a body field is a gate on the CLIENT, and the only client is the one that already drew the sheet — so it guards a caller that has already passed the guard. (2) It would make the API's guard and the sheet's guard two copies of one string that can drift: rename the trip on one device and the other device's cached name no longer arms the delete, which is a failure mode the sheet does not have. (3) The threats it is offered against are `curl`, the slice arc and a future proxy — and for the first two the answer is that they are the developer's own hands on their own stack, while for the third the answer is DEC-86, which closes registration so a stranger cannot hold a token at all. IT IS DECLINED, NOT DISMISSED: the lens's own note that 'an unconfirmed destructive route behind an OPEN registration surface is two gaps that compound' is exactly right, and DEC-86 closes the half that was compounding.
decisions.consequence: R5's work text carries the decline and its reason, so the next worker finds an argument rather than an omission — 'D3 makes you type the name and the API does not' is precisely the asymmetry that otherwise reads as an oversight. THE TRIGGER FOR REVISITING IS NAMED: a second traveller, or any caller of this route that is not the sheet. And the recovery side is strengthened where it actually is thin, which the lens also flagged: R5 builds `DELETE /v1/auth/session` AND a sibling that revokes them all, because a stolen token is the case where you do not know which row to delete.

deferred_decisions.title: How a physical iPhone reaches the local stack
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: A LAN address, a .local name or a tunnel; iOS App Transport Security blocks plain HTTP by default, so it is entangled with whether Caddy serves a certificate the device trusts.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: It depends on a LAN, a certificate story and a device nobody has connected. None of it affects the schema, the API shape or any write.
deferred_decisions.trigger: The first time the Flutter client runs on a physical device against this stack.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: DEC-42's config seam: the address is an env var the signer reads.

deferred_decisions.title: Which hostname the bucket is addressed by, and whether the API and the client use the same one
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: The API reaches MinIO at http://minio:9000 while a phone must reach it at a LAN address; also path-style versus virtual-host-style addressing, which MinIO and real S3 default to differently.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: It is an address, not a design — and R2 builds the seam that makes it an address.
deferred_decisions.trigger: DEF-01, or the first deploy against real S3 or R2.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: S3_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT exists so the two addresses CAN differ without the signer learning about it. The signer only ever sees S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL.

deferred_decisions.title: travellers as a hot row (DBA F21)
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: Every logbook write updates the same travellers row and leaves one dead tuple. Invisible at this size — autovacuum triggers on the threshold of 50, not the scale factor. The DBA did not reproduce it and said so.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: Nothing to measure against. Recording it as a deferral rather than leaving it in a review file is the whole point: the DBA asked for exactly this and it was not written down anywhere until now.
deferred_decisions.trigger: A load test complaining about travellers_pkey bloat.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.0 with threshold = 20, and/or fillfactor = 70 for HOT updates. A storage parameter, not a schema change.

deferred_decisions.title: DEC-02's cross-kind id uniqueness check (DBA F22)
deferred_decisions.deferred_to: unscheduled, and this deferral carries an argument for never
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: The schema permits a city and a trip to share an id — executed, a city with id `autumn-crossing` inserted while that trip existed. The client's Logbook.holdsId refuses it across all five lists AND the nested visits. DEC-58 established the opposite principle for the media reference (a real FK, not a Go check), so this is the one referential rule left living only in Go — except that it does not live in Go either: no six-way EXISTS exists.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: EVERY ID IN THIS SYSTEM IS CLIENT-MINTED, and the client already enforces the rule at the only site that creates one. A server check would duplicate a guarantee at a place that cannot violate it, and PostgreSQL has no extension-free way to express cross-table exclusion, so the alternative is six EXISTS clauses under the advisory lock on every create. The honest position is that DEC-58's precedent does NOT reach here, because there is no constraint to reach for.
deferred_decisions.trigger: The first SERVER-minted id — which would arrive with an import route, a merge, or a second client. At that moment the check is required and the argument above evaporates.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: It is six EXISTS clauses inside a transaction that already holds the traveller's advisory lock, so it is race-free by construction whenever it is written.

deferred_decisions.title: Argon2's parameters, DefaultSessionTTL, and the pool numbers as CHOICES
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: 64 MiB / t=1 / p=4 and thirty days are asserted as VALUES by legs that stop them moving unnoticed. Nothing says they are the right numbers on any machine, and DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS draws on the same RAM Argon2 does.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: DEC-21: local-only target. There is no hardware and no login rate to measure against.
deferred_decisions.trigger: A VPS, or any deploy with a real login rate.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: Every one is a named constant or an environment variable, and Argon2's parameters travel INSIDE the hash — so raising the memory cost does not lock out anybody already registered.

deferred_decisions.title: A media backup, and the ordering it has against the database backup
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: DEC-92 puts a `pg_dump` target in R4 and says nothing about the bucket. Restoring the database alone gives a log whose 308 media references ALL RESOLVE — `cities_cover_fk` and its siblings are satisfied by rows in `media_objects`, which come back with the dump — pointing at bytes that are gone. The failure is not an error anywhere; it is 308 broken images and a foreign-key graph that looks perfectly healthy.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: At fixture scale the bucket is 1.0 MB and two objects, so an `mc mirror` or a volume copy is a one-line addition whenever it is wanted, and nothing about the database backup's shape depends on it. What must not be deferred is the SENTENCE, and it is not: out_of_scope says plainly that a database restore without a bucket restore is a silently broken log.
deferred_decisions.trigger: The first real photograph, or R2 landing on a machine that is not this one.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: DEC-92 already fixes the ORDER for when it lands — bucket first, database second. A dump newer than the bucket copy references objects that were never copied; a bucket copy newer than the dump only leaves unreferenced garbage.

deferred_decisions.title: Reclaiming the two orphan classes, and the zero-code option for one of them
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: MEASURED: every partial or dishonest upload leaves NOTHING in the bucket, so there is exactly ONE orphan class from uploads — a SUCCESSFUL upload that is never committed, leaving `uploaded_at IS NULL` plus a real object, forever. There is a second and larger class the plan did not mention: `media_objects_traveller_fk ON DELETE CASCADE` drops every row when a traveller goes and leaves every object. Both are silent — no log line, no metric, no query.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: OE-12's reasoning stands and is not weakened by this: `Remove` has no caller in R1-R8 and its shape is not knowable until the NOT EXISTS liveness query across four columns exists. What was missing was the ARITHMETIC, and it is now written down: at fixture scale it is 1.0 MB and irrelevant; at 10,000 photographs it is not.
deferred_decisions.trigger: The first real capture, or the bucket passing a size somebody notices.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: A MinIO lifecycle rule expiring objects under a prefix after N days is the ZERO-CODE option for the uncommitted class and is named here as the deferred answer rather than left implicit in an interface that has no method for it.

deferred_decisions.title: Per-resource ETags, and the number that triggers them
deferred_decisions.deferred_to: unscheduled — but the trigger is now a number rather than a feeling
deferred_decisions.what_is_open: `logbook_version` is the whole-log cache key, so a caption edit is one bump and then a full re-read of everything, and the ratio grows without bound with the log. DEC-31 says one read because the log is small; nothing said how small.
deferred_decisions.why_deferred: Below roughly 1 MB the whole-log invalidation is cheaper than any per-resource scheme and DEC-31 is right. DEC-93's cap removes the largest growth term, which is what pushes this out rather than merely postponing it: tracks, not photographs, were the read's real growth term, and the fixture hid it completely with seven points across two walks.
deferred_decisions.trigger: THE EMITTED BODY EXCEEDS THE THRESHOLD AT WHICH A FORCED RE-READ STOPS FITTING THE WriteTimeout BUDGET — which is the same threshold as DEC-94's truncation, and that is why they are one number and not two. MEASURE IT AGAINST THE LINK, NOT THE SERVER: the server side of the 100x re-read is 74.9 ms and the wire side at 1 Mbps is 80 seconds.
deferred_decisions.what_keeps_it_cheap: Nothing in the client changes: it already sends `If-None-Match` and already reads the whole log. The change is entirely server-side and is a new route rather than a modified one.

THE FIVE ACCEPTANCE CHECKS THAT READ `make seed && make check && make slice` ARE REORDERED, AND THAT IS A DOCUMENTATION FIX WITH A REAL FAILURE BEHIND IT (DEC-92). `make slice` runs `docker compose down -v` against the DEFAULT project as step A0 — the same volume `make up`, `make migrate` and `make seed` write — so the documented procedure taught a developer that seeding and then wiping is normal, on a stack that will later hold the only copy of somebody's photographic record. R4, R5, R6, R7 and R8 now read `make check && make slice && make seed`: the fast Docker-free gate, then the arc under its own COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, then the seed on the live stack — which survives. `scripts/check-plan.py` fails on any acceptance check where `make seed` precedes `make slice` on one line, because a convention this document has already got wrong five times in one release is a convention that needs a command rather than a rule.
