steps.work:
1. **ABSENT MEANS LEAVE ALONE, ON EVERY WRITE TYPE** (DEC-89). Every field on every write struct becomes a pointer and a nil field is LEFT ALONE rather than written — exactly as the three sharing flags already are, in a comment one line above the statement that got the other answer for five columns. This makes `createPlace` correct by construction (C1's pin is a wishlist place with no visits) and an accidental re-PUT harmless. IT IS NOT ONE ROUTE: the same convention is what R6 builds `PUT /v1/places/{id}` on, over `visits`, and what R7 builds `PUT /v1/photos/{id}` and `PUT /v1/walks/{id}` on. The measured consequences of each are in DEC-89 and in R6 and R7's own text.
2. **THE THREE LEGS ARE WRITTEN AGAINST THE BODY THE CLIENT ACTUALLY SENDS**, not against a synthesised whole entity — which is the server twin of the client's own rule 'assert on what the widget actually renders'. A name-only trip PUT; a place PUT with `visits` omitted; a walk PUT carrying `{dismissed:true}` alone. The second and third live in R6 and R7 because those routes do not exist yet, and R1 owns the type change and the trip leg.
3. **AND THE ONE ASSERTION THE THREE STANDING GUARDS CANNOT MAKE**: a count that must not fall. `SELECT count(*) FROM photos WHERE place_id IS NOT NULL` is unchanged across every route in R6 and R7 except `refile` (raises it) and the D1/D2-delete branches (lower it by a known amount). The safety lens measured that a caption-only PUT which unfiles a photograph passes ALL THREE current guards green: the dangling check sees no dangling reference, the place-without-occasion check sees no place, and the pair-agreement check sees a pair that agrees. R5's rule — assert on the SURVIVING ROW COUNT, never on error/no-error — is applied here to the routes that do NOT destroy rows.
4. **THE SERVER KEEPS REFUSING A ZONELESS DATE** (DEC-90). `showDatePicker` returns `DateTime(y,m,d)` in the device's local zone, `_addDates` passes it through with no conversion, and `toIso8601String()` emits no zone suffix for a non-UTC value — measured live, `400 invalid_body`, so T4's 'Add dates' fails on every request. The CLIENT converts with `.toUtc()`, and that is a CLIENT-PREREQUISITES item WITH ITS LOCAL CONSEQUENCE SAID OUT LOUD: it changes what `logbook.json` holds, so it is a local-format change as well as a wire one. The server adds a leg asserting the refusal, because guessing at a string's meaning is the class of thing `logbookFormatVersion` exists to refuse. GOLDEN LEGS NEED TWO INPUTS NO FIXTURE CONTAINS: a zoneless string, and a six-digit fraction — `instantLayout` is `.000` and Go TRUNCATES while Dart writes six digits whenever `microsecond != 0`, which `logbookNow()` always has on the VM. Millisecond precision on the wire is the CONTRACT and the client truncates before sending, so the round trip IS byte-identical. `expiresAt` is outside DEC-68's six fields (it emits NINE digits today) and must not be 'fixed' into an Instant.
5. **THE EMITTED TRIP GAINS `shared`** (DEC-91), derived as `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM share_links WHERE traveller_id=$1 AND trip_id=t.id AND revoked_at IS NULL)`. DEC-85 hashes tokens at rest, so the server can no longer emit `Trip.shareLinkId` — and the client-fidelity lens measured that the cost is larger than DEC-85's own estimate: DEC-32's write response is a whole Trip the phone SPLICES into its cache, so an ordinary rename overwrites the local plaintext token with null, H1 renders no URL, and BOTH 'Copy link' and 'Stop sharing' go inert while the row is un-revoked and `GET /l/{token}` still serves it. The user loses the capability AND the only control that revokes it, from an action that has nothing to do with sharing. It is additive with a default, so it does not move the format version by the client's own rule. THE SPLICE MUST BE A MERGE THAT PRESERVES `shareLinkId` RATHER THAN A REPLACEMENT — CLIENT-PREREQUISITES — and H1 gains a THIRD STATE it does not have today: shared, but this device does not hold the link, with 'New link' as the way back, which H1 already offers.
6. **gzip, AND THE READ STOPS BEING BOUNDED ONLY BY WriteTimeout** (DEC-94). `GET /v1/logbook` answers 200 with a valid ETag and a body cut mid-token when body/link-speed exceeds 15s — reproduced three times at three rates against an 11,102,597-byte log. gzip level 1 takes the fixture's 99,271 bytes to 6,806 in 0.3 ms and the 11.1 MB log to 2,084,727 in 47.2 ms. Honour `Accept-Encoding` and SET `Vary`, or the next cache in front of this serves compressed bytes to a client that did not ask. COMPRESSION ALONE DOES NOT REMOVE THE CLASS — it moves the threshold 5-15x — so WriteTimeout is raised and THE CEILING IS SAID OUT LOUD: at 15s the server was promising that no log will ever exceed 15 seconds of the client's downlink, and nothing enforced that. DEC-93's cap removes the largest growth term, which is why the two rulings are worth reading together.
7. **THREE BOUNDS AND A 503** (DEC-96), all in this step and not conditionally in R4. Wire `httpx.Timeout` with a `REQUEST_TIMEOUT` variable at 15s — the middleware is written and has ZERO production call sites, and main.go already states that the only reason it is absent is a missing config variable. Put `statement_timeout=15s` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=60s` on cmd/api's DSN, on the same `options=` line as `search_path=public` — which also closes the divergence DB-MIN-14 found, where migrations create in a pinned schema and the application reads through an unpinned one. Map driver-level connectivity failures (pgconn connect errors, `sql.ErrConnDone`, a pool-acquire deadline) to **503 with `Retry-After: 5`**, leaving 500 for genuine handler faults: a 500 tells a client the server has a bug and the request is poison, when the truth is 'the dependency is down, try again shortly' — and it is unanswerable afterwards, because a 500 count conflates handler bugs with outages. THE ERROR VOCABULARY DOES NOT GROW: this is a status and a header, and DEC-12's twelve codes are untouched.
8. **AND RAISE `start_period` ABOVE `migrateTimeout`** (DEC-96, OPS-MAJ-4). The Dockerfile writes out three nesting budgets (2s < 3s < 4s < 5s) and there is a fourth that does not nest: the server does not listen until migrations finish, `migrateTimeout` allows 120s, and the health budget expires at 3s + 12x5s = 63s. Measured: `health=unhealthy` at t=61s while a CORRECT migration was still waiting for its lock and went on to apply at t=98s — so `make up --wait` fails a deploy that is working, and the natural operator response interrupts a migration mid-flight. `start_period: 150s` costs nothing, because a check that passes during the start period marks the container healthy at once, and the compose file already says that about Postgres.
9. **THE ACCESS LOG LEARNS THREE FIELDS AND LOSES ONE CALLER** (DEC-101). `durationUs` instead of `durationMs` — 15,151 of 15,960 lines over 21.35 hours of the live stack read `durationMs:0`, and the only non-zero values in the whole sample were 4 and 9, so no latency question is answerable from those logs at all. `travellerId` on the request-scoped logger where auth already resolves it (the redactor is keyed on substrings of token/passphrase/authorization, so an id is safe). The MATCHED PATTERN alongside the raw path, because once `/v1/trips/{id}` exists nothing aggregates. And stop access-logging `/healthz` at Info: the disk cost is survivable anywhere, and the signal cost is a 20:1 dilution of the one file you read at 3am. INTO THE DEFINITION OF DONE, for R5-R8: every 500 emits EXACTLY ONE ERROR line carrying the requestId and the underlying error, asserted per handler package by a leg that COUNTS LINES rather than greps for one.
10. Migration 0002 alters `share_photos` and `share_notes` to DEFAULT true, with a comment carrying the client's own sentence about why `share_coordinates` stays false: a pin on your accommodation is not something to hand out by link, so it has to be actively turned on. **IT ALSO BACKFILLS** (DEC-82): `UPDATE trips SET share_photos = true, share_notes = true`, with the reasoning in the file — those rows carry a default the CLIENT NEVER HAD, so they are wrong data rather than a choice, and nothing in the table can distinguish 'written before 0002' from 'the user turned sharing off'. **THE DOWN FILE IS NOT AN INVERSE AND ITS OWN TEXT SAYS SO**: it reverts the two DEFAULTs and deliberately leaves the backfilled rows, because putting everything back to false leaves post-0002 rows wrong in the other direction.
11. `Migrator.Migrate` sets `lock_timeout` on the migration connection, beside the existing `set_config('search_path', …)`. IT IS THE THIRD OF THREE AND NOT THE WHOLE, and v7.1's claim that it closes the stall class is deleted as OE-19.
12. **THE THREE DATE COLUMNS ARE SCANNED INTO `time.Time`** (DEC-102). `v.At`, `p.TakenAt` and `w.RecordedOn` are read out of `sql.NullTime` with `.Valid` never checked — correct today because all three are NOT NULL, but the constraint is doing 100% of the work, and the same file is careful with `instantOrNil` and with `if lat.Valid && lng.Valid`. The driver then errors on a NULL instead of the emitter inventing `0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`, which `DateTime.parse` accepts happily and every screen renders as a year-1 date. One line each, no behaviour change today. **AND CORRECT THE COMMENT WHILE THERE**: one whole-log read is TEN SELECTs, not the six `logbook_store.go`'s own doc comment claims — measured with pg_stat_statements, each `calls = 1`.
13. 0001 IS NOT EDITED. `loadMigrations` checksums `sha256.Sum256(body)` over the whole file, comments included, so any edit — including a comment — raises `ErrChecksumMismatch` against every database that has applied it. Ruling DEC-83 asks for a comment in 0001 and it cannot go there; PD-13 has where it goes instead.
14. **docs/CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md IS CREATED**, for a reader who has NOT read this repository, and v7.2 rewrites its outline because the client-fidelity lens found five items missing and one that is ALREADY DONE. In order: (1) DEC-76's `logbookFormatVersion` -> 2, before the first real request, and the client must SEND `X-Logbook-Format` so a future disagreement is a clean 406 rather than a quarantine. (2) DEC-61's actual consequence, which v7.1 conflated: REGISTER DOES NOT SIGN YOU IN, so it is register-then-session as two separate calls, and the first screen after registering must render a traveller with NO NAME — a state U1 can already draw. Beside it, CF-MIN-11: the register/session responses are their own types and must NOT be decoded with `Traveller.fromJson`, whose `name` is non-nullable while DEC-61 rules that it IS null until `PATCH /v1/me`. (3) DEC-45's platform secure storage as the seventh client dependency — and `dio` is ALREADY in `pubspec.yaml`, so the HTTP client is not a separate conversation; only `flutter_secure_storage` is. (4) PD-16's EIGHTEEN copy sentences in three classes, INCLUDING the one that needs no change. (5) PD-17's twelve-row error table in three lanes. (6) PD-18's `LogbookSource` mapping. (7) DEC-47's ImageProvider keyed by OBJECT ID — promoted from a cache-key argument to the sentence that is actually true: on `wipe/mock-data` there are FIVE `AssetImage` constructions and ZERO declared assets, so without this every image in the app is the failure plate. Name the three answers the client's own record lists as open and unchosen, and say that the decision is now forced rather than deferred. (8) DEC-85's `shareLinkId` consequence and DEC-91's `shared` field, with H1's third state. (9) DEC-88's retry rule: a 412 on the upload PUT means 'already there', NOT 'failed', and the commit path treats it as success. (10) DEC-93's client-side track decimation — the server refusing an over-long track is not the same as the phone knowing to shorten one. (11) DEC-90's `.toUtc()` and its local-format consequence. (12) The `refilePhoto` SIGNATURE CHANGE — it gains `visitId` and `visitAt` because the client mints both, which is a real change to one of the eighteen named methods and to `_freshId`'s role, at one call site, M2.2. (13) DEC-34's cache and the three things logout clears. (14) That the client must not ship a control ahead of its route, because all eighteen unbuilt routes answer `not_found` today and the client's three delete methods are documented to read an unknown id as SUCCESS (RULE-11). **AND ONE ITEM IS STRUCK RATHER THAN LISTED**: the fixture removal and the pinned clock are ALREADY DONE on `wipe/mock-data` — `sample_log.dart` and `assets/imagery/` are deleted and `main.dart`'s own comment records that the `sampleClock` override went with them. Listing it as work sends somebody to undo nothing. State it as 'already done — verify, do not redo'. Every later step appends to this file.

steps.title: internal/media — minio-go behind one interface, a signature that covers the checksum, the type, the size and the key, and a bucket that exists
steps.size: LARGE. A new external dependency, a new compose service, and a signing call that FAILS OPEN.
files: internal/media/store.go        (NEW — PresignPut, PresignGet, Stat, EnsureBucket. NOT Remove; see OE-12)
internal/media/minio.go        (NEW — the one implementation)
internal/media/memory.go       (NEW — the in-memory twin, for handler-level legs)
internal/media/keys.go         (NEW — ONE function returns the key AND the base64 header from one hex digest)
internal/config/config.go      (EDIT — the S3_* variables, MEDIA_MAX_BYTES, and S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC = 15m)
.dockerignore                  (EDIT — patterns, not two exact paths; R2 is where secrets arrive)
deploy/docker-compose.yml      (EDIT — minio at a PINNED tag, its healthcheck, its named volume, api's depends_on, and DEC-95's restart/logging/mem_limit on all three)
deploy/.env.example            (EDIT)
cmd/api/main.go                (EDIT — construct the store and CALL EnsureBucket at boot, the way run() already pings Postgres)

steps.work:
1. `media.Store` declares **PresignPut, PresignGet, Stat and EnsureBucket**, ctx first on every method. `Remove` is deliberately absent — OE-12 — because the sweep that would call it is out of scope and its shape is not knowable until the NOT EXISTS liveness query exists.
2. THE CHECKSUM BAN, and it is the sharpest thing in this step. `PresignedPutObject` and `Presign` both FAIL OPEN: reach for either and no checksum is signed, the upload succeeds, the commit's HEAD succeeds, and a lying client has written arbitrary bytes at an address claiming to be their hash. The URL is minted so the client-supplied SHA-256 is part of what the signature covers, so MinIO — and real S3 — refuse the PUT themselves.
3. **THE LENGTH IS SIGNED THE SAME WAY** (PD-11, and DEC-51 asked for it in these words: `content-length` SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT 'so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping'). v7.0 had an API-side 422 before signing plus a HEAD on commit, and neither binds the holder of the URL: the 422 happens BEFORE the capability is minted, and the HEAD only refuses to MARK the object committed — the bytes are already in the bucket, and nothing in these eight steps reclaims them. `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` joins internal/config with the other eight variables and IT HAS A NUMBER rather than being called 'the bound'.
4. DEC-42's two addresses: `S3_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT` is what the API dials, `S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is what a signature covers and what a phone fetches. They may differ and DEF-02 is why. The signer only ever sees the public one.
5. DEC-47's two lifetimes, **AND THE PUBLIC ONE NOW HAS A NUMBER**: `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PRIVATE` (~2 minutes, the revocation knob, DEC-44) and `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC = 15m` (DEC-84). RULE-07 IS CLOSED and this step is no longer blocked. The ruling also mandates the leg OE-15 deleted the predecessor of, and it is written out in the test strategy rather than described: assert WHICH TTL EACH CALL SITE USES — the private one for `POST /v1/media/mint`, the public one for the URLs `GET /l/{token}` embeds — with a mutation swapping them. v7.1's leg compared the two values to each other, so a handler reaching for the private one would have reddened nothing, and DEC-84 says so in its own words. THE HONEST SENTENCE THE COPY MUST CARRY is the ruling's: stopping a share stops new links at once, and a photograph already loaded may keep working for up to fifteen minutes.
6. MinIO joins compose as the third service — divergence 3 (DEC-39), finally reached. Its healthcheck's timeout goes strictly below its interval, because the compose file shipped violating that rule once and H3 is the leg that caught it. Its bucket is a named volume, for the reason `pgdata` is one.
7. `.dockerignore` gains PATTERNS. It currently names two exact paths — `deploy/.env` and `.env` — and no patterns, so `COPY . .` carries any `.env.local`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_rsa` or `secrets/` into the build stage and the build cache. The existing lines were written to the shape of the file that leaked (the recorded `hunter2-vs1fixes-canary` measurement) rather than to the class, and **R2 is the step that introduces this project's first real secrets**. Add `.env.*`, `!.env.example`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `id_rsa*`, `secrets/`, `.netrc`, `.aws/`.
8. Adopt the dependency only after re-running DEC-43's measurement on the ACTUAL repository rather than the throwaway module: `go mod tidy` must leave `go 1.25.0` alone and build and vet must both exit 0.
9. **NOTHING CREATED THE BUCKET** (DEC-98, STO-BLO-4, OPS-MAJ-7). `MakeBucket` 0 hits and `mc mb` 0 hits across 41 mentions of `bucket` in v7.1. Executed against the official image at a pinned tag with a fresh volume and no init: `/minio/health/live` 200, `/minio/health/ready` 200, `ls /data` -> `.minio.sys` only, ZERO buckets — and `MINIO_DEFAULT_BUCKETS` is a Bitnami variable, not a MinIO one. So R2's acceptance check passed and R4's `make seed` was the first thing to fail, three steps later, with an error that reads like a credentials problem. `EnsureBucket` — `BucketExists` then `MakeBucket` if absent, idempotent — is called AT BOOT in cmd/api, on the same argument `run()` already makes for its Postgres ping: 'a failure here is a real misconfiguration and the process should not come up pretending otherwise'. v7.1 gave media only a nil-check at wiring time. **AND THE DEFINITION OF DONE ASSERTS THE BUCKET RATHER THAN THE PROCESS**: a round-trip PUT+GET inside the `up --wait` arc, because three healthy services against a MinIO that cannot store anything is exactly the fail-open shape this step is careful about for the checksum, arriving through a different door. Add `depends_on: minio: condition: service_healthy` to api, and PIN THE SHIPPED TAG — v7.1 pinned MinIO for the TEST compose file and said nothing about the shipped one, which is pinned backwards in a repo whose compose file already carries a long comment about why an unpinned Postgres tag would silently orphan a named volume.
10. **IT ALSO MAKES R3's 'presigning is a local HMAC' TRUE FROM THE FIRST REQUEST** (STO-MAJ-7), and this is the second reason for doing it at boot rather than in compose. minio-go resolves the bucket region with a REAL NETWORK ROUND TRIP on the first presign per bucket and caches it, so before that cache is warm presigning does I/O and can fail. Two consequences, both closed by the boot call: a wrong `S3_SECRET_KEY` would otherwise start a perfectly healthy server whose every media route 500s, because the wiring-time panic is on nil and not on reachability; and `POST /v1/media/mint` for a twelve-photograph grid would otherwise be one blocking network call plus twelve local HMACs on a cold cache, with no timeout named anywhere. NOTE THE CONTRADICTION THIS RESOLVES, because two lenses measured opposite things: the storage lens got `PresignHeader("no-such-bucket-xyz", …)` -> err 'The specified bucket does not exist' (COLD cache — the region lookup is what failed), while the operations lens and DEC-98 report that presigning against a missing bucket SUCCEEDS and the failure surfaces on the phone as `NoSuchBucket` (WARM cache — offline signing). Both are true, under different preconditions, and `EnsureBucket` at boot removes the question by making the bucket exist and the cache warm before the first request.
11. **CONTENT-TYPE IS SIGNED INTO THE PUT** (DEC-87, STO-MAJ-5). DEC-51's allowlist was described as a defence in three layers and is actually two: the Go 422 and the 0003 CHECK both constrain the DATABASE ROW, while the uploader sets `Content-Type` on the PUT and the bucket keeps it. Executed: PUT with `Content-Type: text/html` -> 200, StatObject -> ct=text/html, presigned GET returns it. So a row reading `image/png`, passing both enforcement points, can address an object the bucket serves as `text/html`. Sign it, from the SAME validated value the 422 and the CHECK see — one function, so the three cannot diverge. Measured working: `SignedHeaders` becomes `content-type;host;x-amz-checksum-sha256`, a mismatched type -> 403, the right one -> 200 with ct preserved. **ACCEPT THE WORSE ERROR**: a legitimate client that guesses its own MIME type wrongly now gets `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch` rather than a 422 naming the field. That is the trade, and the mitigation is DEC-88's `uploadHeaders` map — the client replays what it was given rather than deriving anything.
12. **`If-None-Match: *` IS SIGNED TOO, SO A CONTENT ADDRESS IS WRITE-ONCE AT THE BUCKET** (DEC-88, STO-MAJ-6). The checksum binds the header to the BODY; nothing bound it to the KEY. Executed: a PUT to key `<traveller>/<digestA>` carrying a self-consistent checksum for entirely different bytes B succeeds, and with versioning off a second PUT at a committed key SILENTLY REPLACES the bytes — the address stops holding its own contents. With `If-None-Match: *` signed: first PUT 200, any second 412 PreconditionFailed with the original bytes intact, including that replacement. TWO THINGS FOLLOW AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME THING. (a) `keys.go` holds ONE function returning the key AND the base64 header from one hex digest, so they cannot diverge; a mutation computing them from two variables reddens a leg. (b) THE RETRY STORY GOES IN CLIENT-PREREQUISITES OR THIS IS A REGRESSION: a client re-uploading after an unacknowledged success gets 412, which means 'already there', NOT 'failed', and the commit path treats it as success. **AND ONE THING THAT IS FREE AND SHOULD BE TAKEN**: `StatObject` with `Checksum: true` returns the stored digest, so commit verifies the DIGEST as well as the size at no extra call — and an object uploaded through the BANNED call has an EMPTY checksum, which turns the ban from a grep into a RUNTIME guard. Note the flag: without `Checksum: true` the field is silently empty and the check passes nothing.
13. **THE OPERATIONS HYGIENE THAT BELONGS WITH THE THIRD SERVICE** (DEC-95). `restart: always` on all services, with the reason in the compose file's own voice: `unless-stopped` does not restart a container stopped from OUTSIDE and that decision persists across daemon restart and host reboot — measured as a controlled pair, a container that dies on its own reaches `restarting restarts=6` in 20s while one killed by a human sits at `exited restarts=0` indefinitely, and on the real service `docker kill` left Postgres exited 100+ seconds later while the API sat at `healthy` and every request 500'd. `logging: {driver: json-file, options: {max-size: 10m, max-file: 3}}` on all three: `LogConfig.Config` is empty on both containers today and json-file runs uncapped at 3.4 MB/day = 1.26 GB/year, of which 94.9% is the healthcheck talking to itself. `mem_limit` per service, so the OOM-killer's choice is yours rather than 'whichever has the largest RSS' — which, AFTER THIS STEP, is MinIO and not the API. The three numbers go into docs/BEFORE-A-PUBLIC-DEPLOY.md as the sizing derivation: API 140.5 MiB steady after one Argon2 run (12.42 idle, and it does NOT come back down, so each +1 on ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT is +64 MiB of steady working set), MinIO 214.7 MiB idle, Postgres at its default 128 MB shared_buffers. A 1 GiB VPS is roughly half-spent before any data.

steps.work:
1. POST /v1/media takes {sha256, byteSize, contentType} and answers **{id, uploadUrl, expiresAt, alreadyExists, uploadHeaders}**. `alreadyExists` derives from `uploaded_at IS NOT NULL`. **`uploadHeaders` IS DEC-88's AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL** (STO-BLO-2): a presigned PUT whose signature covers `x-amz-checksum-sha256`, `Content-Type` and `If-None-Match` is UNUSABLE unless the caller replays each one exactly — and the checksum's value is the BASE64 digest while `id` and the wire format are HEX. Measured: header omitted -> 400 AccessDenied, object absent; header present with the wrong value -> 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch; header present and correct -> 200. A Flutter client handed only `uploadUrl` gets a 400 on every upload, forever, with no way to derive the required header from the response. So the map is a flat `{header: value}` with the values ALREADY ENCODED SERVER-SIDE, the client replays it verbatim and never re-derives an encoding, and **THE LEG THAT KEEPS THEM HONEST IS THAT THE MAP'S KEY SET EQUALS THE URL's `X-Amz-SignedHeaders` MINUS `host`** — parsed out of the URL, so the two cannot drift when a fourth header is signed.
2. **THE UPSERT'S CONFLICT BRANCH IS BOUNDED**, which v7.0 never specified: `... DO UPDATE SET byte_size = EXCLUDED.byte_size, content_type = EXCLUDED.content_type WHERE media_objects.uploaded_at IS NULL`. Without the WHERE, a client re-beginning an already-committed digest rewrites the declared type and size of bytes it no longer controls — executed by the database lens: a committed row `(10 | image/png)` became `(999999 | text/html)`, and migration 0003's allowlist does not close it because any allowlisted-but-wrong type passes. With the WHERE the row is untouched.
3. **AND RECORD WHY THE DELETED `RETURNING` CANNOT COME BACK.** v6 deleted it as OE-4 with the reason 'not an xmax trick', which leaves the door open. The real reason, executed: `DO UPDATE … WHERE <false>` and `DO NOTHING` both return ZERO ROWS (`INSERT 0 0`, no row emitted), so a handler reading its answer off RETURNING gets nothing on exactly the `alreadyExists` path. A separate SELECT is correct and is race-free under `WithTravellerLock`.
4. POST /v1/media/{id}/commit HEADs the bucket, verifies the size, sets `uploaded_at`. 409 `upload_incomplete` when the object is not there. This is PD-05's first Service operation.
5. POST /v1/media/mint takes a LIST of ids and answers a list of URLs. No singular GET (OE-1), no batch store method (OE-2) — presigning is a local HMAC, so the loop is in the handler.
6. **THE ALLOWLIST IS `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$`, WRITTEN OUT HERE** (PD-10, DEC-51). v7.0 named the constraint and deferred the list to the worker, so the schema check could not be written and all three layers of the anti-XSS defence were absent at once. Enforced TWICE on DEC-58's precedent: in Go for the 422 naming the field, and as an IN-list in 0003. `image/png` and `image/jpeg` are load-bearing beyond the fixture — `schema_test.go:62` seeds shared helpers with `image/jpeg`, so omitting it breaks every leg using them. RULE-09 asks whether `heic` should be there at all; this plan enumerates DEC-51 as ruled.
7. **`response-content-disposition: attachment` ON EVERY PRESIGNED GET.** DEC-51 states the defence as the disposition PLUS the allowlist, with the residual named: a mislabelled object is downloaded, never rendered. v7.0 had neither, while keeping V4-SF3's correct removal of `nosniff` — which S3's closed response-header override set cannot produce. Carry V4-SF3's reasoning forward in a comment so it is not re-litigated.
8. **DEC-51's HEADERS ARE APPLIED FROM THE ROUTE TABLE** (PD-09), not from a path-prefix guess in middleware. `Route` gains `NoStore bool` and `Limit`. R3 asserts `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on `POST /v1/media/mint`; R8 asserts the same on `GET /l/{token}`, which is the case DEC-51's own evidence paragraph names and which v7.0 wired into the step that does not build it.
9. Migration 0003 also carries three things the database lens found while it was open: `media_objects_uploaded_after_created_ck CHECK (uploaded_at IS NULL OR uploaded_at >= created_at)` — a row could be committed ten years before it was created, executed, and the sweep's grace window keys off exactly these timestamps; four `IS NULL OR <> ''` CHECKs on `photos.caption`, `visits.note`, `trips.summary` and `places.plan`, which `travellers.name` and `walks.name` already have and which R7 enforces in Go only; and **`COMMENT ON COLUMN photos.place_id` / `photos.visit_id`** carrying ruling DEC-83 (PD-13 — it cannot go in 0001, and a catalog comment is better than a `--` comment anyway).
10. **THE CONSTRAINT RENAME IS A CATALOG-LEG CHANGE.** 0003 replaces `media_objects_content_type_present_ck` with `media_objects_content_type_ck`, and 0001's own header warns that a rename moves a name the catalog legs assert. `internal/postgres/schema_test.go:690` asserts the old one, which is why that file is in this step's list — v7.0's was not.
11. **OE-10 IS RE-EXAMINED, AS v7.0 PROMISED, AND IT STANDS.** `POST /v1/media/mint` is the POST that writes nothing, so `Mutating == (Method != GET)` does stop holding here — but nothing reads `Mutating`, and two fields arriving that ARE read (`NoStore`, `Limit`) is not an argument for keeping a third that is not.
12. **A NO-TRANSACTION MIGRATION MUST BE PROVED RE-RUNNABLE, AND R3 IS WHERE THE PROOF LANDS** (DEC-99, OPS-BLO-2). A `-- migrate:no-transaction` file that fails part way is an UNRECOVERABLE BOOT LOOP: the runner applies statements 1..i, writes no `schema_migrations` row, and every subsequent boot re-runs from statement 1 — failing on an already-applied statement with a DIFFERENT error that HIDES THE ORIGINAL FAULT, forever, under DEC-95's `restart: always`. Executed against the real Migrator with a three-statement 0003: run 1 reported `statement 3 … ERROR: division by zero`; runs 2 and 3, byte-identical file, both reported `statement 2 … ERROR: relation "probe_half_applied" already exists`. The actual fault is not reachable from any run after the first. Four things, and R3 owns them because R3 is the step that introduces 0003: (a) a test that runs every no-transaction migration TWICE against the same database and requires the second run to be clean — that is what 're-runnable' MEANS and it is mechanically checkable; (b) an `IF NOT EXISTS` / `DROP … IF EXISTS` requirement stated in the file header and greppable; (c) a documented recovery in this step: the exact psql to inspect `schema_migrations`, plus the `DROP INDEX` for the INVALID index `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` leaves behind on failure; (d) the failure message carries the version AND THE STATEMENT TEXT, not just the ordinal, so log line one is enough. **AND THE HONEST PART, WHICH MUST BE WRITTEN OR THE GUARD IS VACUOUS**: 0003 AS SPECIFIED IS ENTIRELY TRANSACTIONAL and carries no directive at all, so today the twice-run test has no real subject. It is written against a FIXTURE migration in `testdata` that does carry the directive, and that is precisely why it goes in now rather than with the first `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` — a guard written after the incident is a cleanup. A test whose subject set is empty is a green that means nothing, so the leg asserts the subject set is NON-EMPTY before running it.
13. **THE COMMIT SEAM IS THE ONLY NON-ATOMIC ONE IN THE PLAN, AND IT GETS A RETRY CONTRACT** (SAF-MIN-12). Every destructive path in R5, R6 and R7 is a single transaction and cannot half-apply — the safety lens could not construct a partial cascade. The one seam that can is bucket-versus-database, and it appears twice. Here: 'HEAD the bucket, verify, mark uploaded' — the bucket confirms, the database update fails, and the object exists with `uploaded_at` NULL, which R7's photo route then rejects, so the user has uploaded bytes they cannot attach and no route to retry that says so. **A SECOND COMMIT OF AN ALREADY-UPLOADED OBJECT IS A 200 AND NOT A 409**, so a client that lost the response can just ask again. And a note goes into `next_slice`'s sweep design: the grace window exists for exactly this state, so it must be measured from the media row's `created_at` and not from anything in the bucket.
14. **WHAT THE PUBLIC ENVELOPE'S URLs ARE** (STO-MIN-12), one sentence, written here because R3 is where minting is built and R8 is where it is embedded: a presigned URL is 394 characters, so twelve in one envelope is roughly 4.7 kB of JSON, and it is a PURE BEARER CAPABILITY — unlimited replay, and unsigned request headers such as `Range` are accepted. That is what makes `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` load-bearing rather than hygiene: it is what keeps the capability out of the next site's logs.

steps.work:
1. `logbook.RewriteAssets` (PD-03) maps the two locators to the two digests across FOUR columns and REFUSES an unmapped one, naming it.
2. internal/seed/fixture.go turns a rewritten `logbook.Document` into a `seed.Dataset` — the types already exist and already mirror the schema. Two mappings need care and both are load-bearing: VISIT ORDINALS must be assigned in the fixture's own array order, because the client reads `visits.first.at` as lastVisited and the fixture is newest-first; and trip_cities ordinals in cityIds order, because that list is travel order.
3. **THE REFUSAL IS ONE PREDICATE AND IT IS THE SAME ONE DEC-86 PUTS ON REGISTER: refuse when ANY TRAVELLER ROW EXISTS** (DEC-97), not 'when the log is non-empty'. It covers both directions and removes the ambiguity v7.1 left unspecified — whether a registered traveller with no writes counts as empty. A SECOND GUARD THE PLAN DID NOT HAVE: refuse unless an explicit `--i-know-this-is-a-dev-database` marker is present, because the DSN alone cannot tell a dev database from a production one, and PD-02's required `-dsn` with no environment fallback is kept. **PRINT THE DSN AND THE TRAVELLER ID IN THE REFUSAL AS WELL AS IN THE SUCCESS** (SAF-MAJ-8), so an operator who has pointed at the wrong database learns it from the refusal. internal/seed.Load inserts in dependency order inside ONE transaction, and refuses rather than merging. It sets logbook_version to 1 so that the first read has a valid ETag — a traveller at 0 is served 200 with no ETag by design, which is correct for a log nobody has written and wrong for one that was just loaded.
4. It uploads the two PNGs through internal/media and commits them through the same path POST /v1/media/{id}/commit uses (ruling DEC-78), so a seeded object is indistinguishable from an uploaded one.
5. **IT CREATES ONE TRAVELLER AND ITS PASSPHRASE IS GENERATED PER RUN** (DEC-97, OPS-BLO-3). v7.1 said 'a known address and passphrase, printed on completion', and DEC-86 — ruled after R4 was written — closes `POST /v1/auth/register` once any traveller row exists. Together they lock the owner out of their own deployment with a published credential: `make up && make seed` is the obvious first thing an operator types, R4's refusal was scoped to 'a non-empty LOG' and a freshly migrated database IS empty, and the result is a deployment whose only account has a passphrase printed in a terminal and checked into a fixture, carrying a 600/min budget, with registration closed so the real traveller can never create theirs.
6. **DEC-70's PROOF METHOD (b) IS NOT USED, AND ITS STATED REASON IS CORRECTED** (OE-13). `SET enable_seqscan=off` is vacuous for every index on `photos`: the planner picks any index leading on `traveller_id` and filters, so the assertion passes with the intended index deleted — executed, `Index Scan using photos_asset_idx … Filter: (visit_id = …)`, the wrong index, before any mutation, and still green after `DROP INDEX photos_visit_idx`. The catalog leg is the sole load-bearing proof and EVIDENCE.md says so. **AND THE REPLACEMENT IS BETTER THAN WHAT DEC-70 PERMITS**: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF) DELETE FROM trips …` prints `Trigger for constraint trip_cities_trip_fk: time=0.248 calls=1` and the same for all five cascades, by name, with timings — so DEC-70's sentence that RI checks 'NEVER appear in EXPLAIN, not even under ANALYZE' is false, even though its conclusion (you cannot assert the plan changed, because the plan INSIDE the trigger is not shown) holds. R4 records the trigger lines: which cascades fired and what each cost is a real reproducible measurement.
7. `internal/seed/generate.go` stays a stub, and its comment gains one sentence with arithmetic: a single multi-row INSERT of 50,000 photographs at 13 written columns is 650,000 bind parameters, well over the wire protocol's int16 count, so the generator chunks and the 284-row seed does not need to. Measured at fixture scale for contrast: the whole ten-table load is 15.1 ms server-side, 744 kB on disk.
8. **`cmd/api`'s DSN gains `options=`.** The migration runner pins `search_path` and the test harness pins it in the DSN; `cmd/api` does neither, so migrations create in a pinned schema and the application reads through an unpinned one — two resolutions, and the application's is the untested one. Executed: connecting as the compose role gives `SHOW search_path` -> `"$user", public`, which works today only because no schema named `travellog` exists and PostgreSQL silently skips a missing entry. `auth_store.go:58` resolves `lower` through whatever the session's path happens to be — the risk 0001's own header measured and attributed to the runner's pin, but the runner is not the runtime. Honest on reachability: shadowing `lower` needs CREATE on a schema in the path, so this is defence in depth rather than a live exploit; it is one line, and it removes a divergence between where migrations write and where the app reads. **THIS WHOLE ITEM MOVED TO R1 AND IS DELETED HERE (OE-16).** DEC-96 chose the numbers — `statement_timeout=15s` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=60s` — and put them on the same `options=` line in the SAME STEP as `lock_timeout`, with the reason stated plainly: 'a number chosen and written beats a number deferred'. DEF-03 is deleted with it. What is left for R4 is nothing: the line is R1's.
9. docs/EVIDENCE.md gains DEC-70's honest limit — measured here, at 284 rows, because this is the first step with 284 rows: which of the mandated indexes the planner actually chooses during a full trip cascade, and the statement that almost none of them are chosen at this size and that this is CORRECT rather than a reason to delete one.
10. **A BACKUP, AND `make slice` STOPS BEING ABLE TO DESTROY THE LIVE VOLUME** (DEC-92, SAF-BLO-3, OPS-MAJ-6). R4 IS WHERE THE VOLUME STOPS BEING DISPOSABLE, which is why it is here: the plan's own premise is that PostgreSQL is the record and the phone is a cache, and across all 261 KB of v7.1 `pg_dump` had 0 hits, `backup` 0, `rotat` 0. THREE THINGS. (a) `make backup`: `docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -Fc -U travellog travellog > backups/travellog-<date>.dump` — custom format so `pg_restore` survives a minor version bump — keep 7. (b) **ONE RESTORE REHEARSAL, RUN ONCE, WITH ITS OUTPUT RECORDED IN EVIDENCE.md.** A backup nobody has restored is not a backup, and this project already holds that standard for everything else. (c) `make slice` runs under its own `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` and REFUSES the live project unless `SLICE_DESTROY_VOLUME=1`. The arc already runs two of its five phases that way — `phase_testdb` and `phase_healthcheck` — so the main phase using the live project is the inconsistency and not the pattern; `scripts/slice-arc.sh:38` builds COMPOSE with no `-p` and step A0 at :389-390 is a bare `down -v` with no prompt, no `--yes` and no guard variable anywhere in 700+ lines. **AND THE FIVE ACCEPTANCE CHECKS ARE REORDERED**: R4, R5, R6, R7 and R8 read `make check && make slice && make seed` rather than `make seed && make check && make slice`, because the documented procedure taught a developer that seeding and then wiping is normal. `scripts/check-plan.py` fails on the old order, because a convention this document got wrong five times in one release needs a command rather than a rule. **WHEN R2's BUCKET IS IN THE PICTURE THE ORDER IS FIXED**: back up the BUCKET first and the DATABASE second. A dump newer than the bucket copy references objects that were never copied; a bucket copy newer than the dump only leaves unreferenced garbage. The media backup itself is DEF-07 and is not built here — and out_of_scope carries the honest sentence, that a database restore without a bucket restore is a SILENTLY broken log.
11. **THE TWO NUMBERS THIS PLAN CARRIED WRONGLY ARE CORRECTED WHERE THEY ARE MEASURED** (DEC-102). The emitted body at fixture scale is **99,271 bytes**, not 85,422 — that second figure is the CLIENT's format-1 file, and DEC-46's 64-hex ids replaced 31-32 character bundle paths across 284 photographs plus three cover columns. Every size argument in v7.0 and v7.1 was ~16% optimistic and the drift is STRUCTURAL rather than a one-off: it grows with the photograph count, and it is the number DEC-31 rests on. And one whole-log read is **TEN** SELECTs, not six — photos, visits, trip_cities, places, cities, trips, walk_points, walks, logbook_version, traveller name, each with `calls = 1`. Ten is also what makes the 3 ms 304 legible: nine round trips at roughly 0.3 ms over 0.176 ms of actual server work, so it is round trips and not work. R4's acceptance check RECORDS the emitted size rather than asserting the old one. **AND STATE THE GO/SQL SPLIT SO NOBODY OPTIMISES THE WRONG HALF**: at 100x, 37.06 ms of a 61.20 ms read is Postgres and 24.1 ms is row-to-struct scanning through database/sql. The query plans are already sane and the planner is right to decline indexes on the small tables.
12. **AND ONE CONSEQUENCE OF DEC-57 THAT NOBODY WROTE DOWN** (SAF-MAJ-8). Nothing in this application can delete a city. DEC-57 made that deliberate and correct on the destructive side — the client has no delete-a-city control, so no user-facing sentence authorises a cascade — but it means a log that acquires 12 cities acquires them permanently. Exhausting every control the client has (D2 on all 17 places with `?photos=delete`, D3 on all 7 trips) clears photographs, places, visits and walks and leaves 12 cities and 2 media objects standing with no route, no sheet and no control able to touch them. So a seed run against the wrong DSN leaves a permanent residue of somebody else's geography in the user's record — which is what DEC-97's second guard is for, and it is recorded in CLAUDE.md beside DEC-57 because an unstated consequence is exactly how the missing FK indexes got there.

DELETE /v1/trips/{id} implements D3's own table exactly and nothing more: the trip goes; its photographs and their notes go; its walks go; every place SURVIVES, minus that trip's visits, INCLUDING a place left with zero visits, which is a wishlist place and is what the sheet promised; the cities are untouched; the link dies because the link is on the trip. It answers the WHOLE LOGBOOK, because the cache cannot splice a cascade.
2. The server-side `_repointed`: after the cascade no surviving photograph names a visit that has gone. The schema does this through `ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)` — which exists only because the DBA found it — and the leg asserts it rather than trusting it.
3. PUT /v1/trips/{id}/share writes only the flags that were sent. POST mints a link the CLIENT supplies and revokes the current row in the SAME TRANSACTION (DEC-67). DELETE revokes AND resets all three flags EXPLICITLY to true/true/false — an UPDATE does not see a DEFAULT, so PD-01's migration does not do this for you.
4. DELETE /v1/auth/session revokes this token, **and it gains a sibling that revokes them all**. The security lens's argument is short and right: a stolen token is precisely the case where you do not know which row to delete, and 'this token' is the one thing the thief will not use. Against a thirty-day untuned TTL that is the only recovery a user has. The client has no control that calls either — which goes in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES rather than being a reason not to build them.
4b. **THE RATE-LIMIT HOLE THIS STEP WOULD HAVE INHERITED IS ALREADY FIXED**, in code, at `d5be39c`, because it was reachable NOW rather than when built: `Mount` applied limiting and authentication as either/or, so every authenticated route had no limit at all — measured, sixty concurrent `GET /v1/logbook` drew sixty 200s. It now composes as `authed(perTraveller(handler))` with `TRAVELLER_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` (600) keyed on the traveller id, so config carries EIGHT variables and not seven. Recorded here because R5's routes are the first destructive ones to arrive behind it, and because a fix that landed between plan revisions is exactly the kind a later reader assumes was planned.
5. docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md is WRITTEN HERE: the exact key set at every level, the row-filtering rules, and what each of the three flags removes. Written by somebody holding the flags and not holding R8's handler, which is the whole of DEC-24's argument.
6. **SHARE TOKENS ARE HASHED AT REST** (DEC-85), which is migration 0004 and is why the migration count is four. `share_links.token_hash bytea` replaces the plaintext column, sha256 of the raw token, constant-time compared — the same shape `sessions` already uses — and `share_links_token_key` becomes a unique index on the hash. DEC-10's plaintext half is REVERSED: under DEC-67's revoke-and-keep design a dump holds EVERY capability ever issued, live and revoked, and hashing costs that design nothing. **THE COST IS REAL AND IT IS LARGER THAN THE RULING'S OWN ESTIMATE**, which the client-fidelity lens measured: the server can no longer emit `Trip.shareLinkId`, and because DEC-32's write response is a whole Trip the phone splices into its cache, an ordinary rename destroys the local plaintext token. DEC-91's `shared` field is the answer and it lands in R1. **AND RE-DERIVE DEC-67 WHILE HERE**, as the ruling asks: its history argument rests on 'DEC-10 stores the token in plaintext', which DEC-85 has just made false. The revoked-vs-unknown 404 is unaffected and PD-12's equal-work requirement still applies.
7. **REGISTRATION CLOSES AFTER THE FIRST TRAVELLER** (DEC-86). `POST /v1/auth/register` refuses once any traveller row exists. It is one line and it removes the whole question rather than bounding it, and it lands here with the other auth work rather than in `next_slice` — the human took it, so it is scope. NOTE THE ORACLE SHRINKS RATHER THAN GROWS: the 409-on-duplicate the security lens flagged as an enumeration surface becomes a 409-on-any-second-registration, which tells an attacker only that the instance is in use, which the login page already tells them. It also pairs with DEC-97 in R4 — the two together were what locked the owner out, and R4 has the other half.
8. **TouchSession LEAVES THE TRAVELLER'S ADVISORY LOCK AND BECOMES GRANULAR** (DEC-100). Measured with pg_stat_statements reset around exactly one 304: NINE database round trips, FIVE of them to stamp a timestamp — `begin`, `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, `SELECT 1 FROM travellers`, `UPDATE sessions SET last_used_at`, `commit` — total server exec 0.176 ms against a 3.0-4.0 ms wall clock, so it is round trips and not work. It also SERIALISES against the phone's own in-flight writes through the same lock. `tx.go`'s comment argues at length that sessions must not bump `logbook_version`, which is correct and is a DIFFERENT QUESTION from whether they should take the write lock. Take it out of `WithTravellerLock` — it writes one row keyed by session id and the lock buys it nothing the row lock does not, and the existence check the wrapper performs for it is a whole extra row read per request that the UPDATE's own `WHERE traveller_id` already answers. Write `last_used_at` only when the stored value is more than a few minutes old, which turns a per-request write into a per-hour one. Nothing in this project depends on it being exact.
9. **THE NAME-CONFIRMATION GATE ON `DELETE /v1/trips/{id}` IS DECLINED, AND THE REASON IS HERE RATHER THAN IN A LENS REPORT** (PD-22, SAF-MAJ-7). D3 is the most guarded control in the client — four itemised consequences beside the words 'deleted' and 'kept', and then the user types the trip's name out before the action arms — and this route requires a bearer token and nothing else. The lens offers two branches and this plan takes the second, which the lens names: say so here, with the reason. THE GATE THE SHEET HAS IS A GATE ON THE HUMAN and its value is the pause before the typing; a body field is a gate on the CLIENT, and the only client is the one that already drew the sheet. It would also make the API's guard and the sheet's guard two copies of one string that can drift — rename the trip on one device and the other device's cached name no longer arms the delete, which is a failure the sheet does not have. And the threat it is offered against is largely closed elsewhere: DEC-86 shuts registration, so a stranger cannot hold a token at all, and the lens's own note that 'an unconfirmed destructive route behind an OPEN registration surface is two gaps that compound' is exactly right about the half that was compounding. TRIGGER FOR REVISITING: a second traveller, or any caller of this route that is not the sheet.
10. **THE SHARE-RESET MUTATION v7.1 NAMED GOES GREEN, SO IT IS REPLACED** (DB-MAJ-4). `UPDATE … SET col = DEFAULT` is legal SQL, it reaches the column default, and after migration 0002 it produces exactly true/true/false — the correct answer. So the mutation proves nothing and the sentence 'a DEFAULT does not reach an UPDATE' is stated too broadly: it is true only of an UPDATE THAT DOES NOT NAME THE COLUMN. The leg is right and is kept; the mutation becomes one that can actually redden — implement the reset as a bare UPDATE touching only `share_links` and not the flags at all. This is defect class 9 landing on a mutation nobody ran.
11. **AND ONE THING DEC-67's OWN ARGUMENT DOES NOT SURVIVE, DECIDED IN WRITING RATHER THAN BY SILENCE** (SAF-MIN-9). `share_links_trip_fk` is ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting a trip destroys the whole revocation history for that trip, revoked rows included — and DEC-67 chose `PRIMARY KEY (traveller_id, token)` over the natural key specifically to keep that history. It is ACCEPTED: the trip is gone, so 'which token was live on a trip that no longer exists' is not a question anyone asks, and D3's sheet could not reasonably itemise a server-side artefact the client's model never held. The decision goes in 0004's own comment beside DEC-85's, because 0001 cannot be edited — so the next reader finds the two arguments together rather than in contradiction.

steps.work:
1. PUT /v1/cities/{id} is createCity. With `attachTo` it also appends the new id to that trip's cityIds IN THE SAME TRANSACTION and is therefore CASCADING — it answers the whole logbook. Country is two columns (DEC-59) and comes from the request, because the client's geocoder supplies it and the user never types it.
2. PUT /v1/places/{id} carries the WHOLE ORDERED visits array. Ordinals are assigned from the array's position, and the array is newest-first because that is what the client sends and reads.
2b. **AND THE WRITE IS AN UPSERT, NOT A DELETE-THEN-INSERT** (PD-06). This reverses what four documents said — 0001's header mandates delete-then-insert in capitals, the shipped `replaceTripCities` is named as the pattern to copy, the prior DBA pass wrote 'the same strategy applies and the same proof covers it' about visits specifically, and v7.0's own leg list called this 'the delete-then-insert reorder'. It is safe on `trip_cities`, which has no referencing child. `visits` has one: `photos_visit_fk … ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)`. Reproduced on the live postgres:17 — delete a place's visits and re-insert the two IDENTICAL rows in one transaction, and the photograph filed there comes back `ph-1 | fushimi-inari | (null)`. **A NO-OP RE-SEND OF AN UNCHANGED ARRAY DESTROYS THE FILING**, silently, with no count moving and `DELETE 2 / INSERT 0 2` as the only trace. THE SHAPE, executed and verified to preserve the filing: `UPDATE visits SET ordinal = ordinal + 1000 WHERE traveller_id=$1 AND place_id=$2`, then `INSERT … ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT visits_pkey DO UPDATE SET ordinal = EXCLUDED.ordinal, …`, then DELETE only the ids absent from the incoming array. **THE OFFSET GOES UPWARD AND THAT IS NOT A PREFERENCE**: downward violates `visits_ordinal_ck CHECK (ordinal >= 0)` (executed: `new row for relation "visits" violates check constraint "visits_ordinal_ck"`), and the set-based `SET ordinal = 1 - ordinal` collides on the non-deferrable UNIQUE because it is checked per ROW during a statement. Making the constraint DEFERRABLE was declined for 0001's own stated reason: it moves the 422 to `tx.Commit()`.
3. DELETE /v1/places/{id}?photos=keep|delete — THE PARAMETER IS REQUIRED, not defaulted. A default is a silent answer to the question D2 makes the user answer on screen.
4. D2's DELETE BRANCH IS STATEMENT ORDER AND NOT A FOREIGN KEY, and this is PD-05's second Service operation. The photographs must be deleted BEFORE the place: delete the place first and `ON DELETE SET NULL (place_id)` clears their place_id, and the delete then matches nothing. Two lines whose order silently inverts the sheet's promise.
5. D2's KEEP branch is the foreign key: the photographs lose their pin and their occasion together and keep their date and city — which is exactly `Photo.copyWith(clearPlace: true)`, and it is executable only because of the column-list form the DBA found.
6. THE WALKS ARE NOT TOUCHED. There is no place_id on walks, and that absence is D2's 'the track stays with the day it was recorded either way'. The leg asserts the walk count is unchanged on BOTH branches.
7. **A BARE `Place` MARSHALS `"visits":null` AND THE CLIENT THROWS** (CF-BLO-3, PD-15). `PUT /v1/places/{id}` answers a Place, and `place.g.dart:33-35` reads `(json['visits'] as List<dynamic>)` — non-nullable, no null branch. This is the `"cityIds":null` defect that `emit.go`'s own comment records as having cost a defect against the running server, arriving in the next step that answers a bare entity. `EmitPlace` lands here, and **THE AST SWEEP THE DEFINITION OF DONE PROMISES IS WRITTEN HERE RATHER THAN IN R8**, because R6 is the FIRST step that can violate the rule and a sweep written after five steps of violations is a cleanup. CITY NEEDS NONE AND THE REASON IS STATED: `City` carries no list field, so there is no nil slice for the marshaller to write as null — measured, bare `City` carries no list key at all. Adding an `EmitCity` for symmetry would be the empty forwarding method DEC-62 warns against one layer up.
8. **ABSENT `visits` IS NOT `visits: []`, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE WHOLE OF THE REMAINING HAZARD** (DEC-89, SAF-MAJ-4). PD-06's upsert fix closes the no-op re-send and does NOT close the empty or omitted array: the mandated shape ends 'then DELETE only the ids absent from the incoming array', and WHEN THE INCOMING ARRAY IS EMPTY OR ABSENT, EVERY ID IS ABSENT — so it does exactly what delete-then-insert did, with the fix in place. Measured: an empty visits array unfiles 30 photographs across 3 trips at Fushimi alone, 95 whole-log, while every count except one stays put. THE CONTRACT: **`visits` absent = do not touch the visits at all**, which makes `createPlace` correct by construction (C1's pin is a wishlist place with no visits, and 'a place with no visits IS a wishlist place' is the client's own sentence) and makes an accidental re-PUT harmless; **`visits: []` = an explicit request to clear, which no client control issues, so it is REFUSED with a 422 naming the field until one exists**. 'A sheet describing a choice the model cannot offer is worse than a sheet offering less' cuts both ways, and a route offering a destruction no sheet authorises is the same error. THE LEG: PUT a place with the `visits` key OMITTED and assert all 28 survive and all 30 photographs keep their filing; PUT with `visits: []` and assert 422 with `field: visits` and NOTHING removed.
9. **THE COUNT THAT MUST NOT FALL, ON THIS STEP'S THREE ROUTES** (DEC-89). `SELECT count(*) FROM photos WHERE place_id IS NOT NULL` is unchanged across `PUT /v1/cities/{id}` and `PUT /v1/places/{id}`, and falls by a KNOWN amount on `DELETE /v1/places/{id}` — known, not merely non-zero, because the fixture's numbers make it writable and R4 measures them. The three standing guards cannot make this assertion: the dangling check sees no dangling reference, the place-without-occasion query sees no place, and the pair-agreement assertion sees a pair that agrees.
10. **THE VISITS WRITE IS ONE STATEMENT PER PHASE, NOT ONE PER ROW** (PERF-MIN-8). `PutTrip` is two round trips per child inside the advisory lock — one `SELECT 1 FROM cities` per city id, then one INSERT per city — which is irrelevant for trips (five cities at worst in the fixture) and is not for a place: the fixture already holds one with 28 visits and a real ten-year log would hold more. Do the existence check as one `= ANY($2)` and the insert as one multi-row INSERT. NOTE THE WIRE-PROTOCOL CAP the database lens found: 65,535 bind parameters, so batch rather than assuming one statement always fits.

#   -> 0, before AND after re-sending every place unchanged. It is 0 in the client's

steps.title: Photographs and walks — the caption, the delete, the bulk snooze, and a re-file that honours the occasion the client chose
steps.size: LARGE — five routes, and one of them is the most intricate write in the system

steps.work:
1. PUT /v1/photos/{id} is setPhotoCaption, and it validates that `asset` names a COMMITTED object — the Go check exists to produce a 422 naming the field, and photos_asset_fk is what actually guarantees it. Empty or whitespace caption stores NULL and never the empty string, because that is what the client does.
2. DELETE /v1/photos/{id} is non-cascading: 204 and a new ETag. Nothing points at a photograph.
3. POST /v1/photos/snooze is the first route taking a COLLECTION, so it is the first place a partial failure has to answer for a group. All-or-nothing in ONE transaction with ONE version bump; an unknown photo id in the list is SKIPPED rather than fatal, matching the client's own method. An EMPTY match writes nothing and says so.
4. POST /v1/photos/{id}/refile is PD-05's third Service operation, and it VALIDATES rather than re-derives. The client mints both the placeId and, when the occasion is new, the visitId and its `at` — so the server's job is to check them, not to choose. It REFUSES a place in another city. It sets place_id and visit_id TOGETHER, always — **and ruling DEC-83 says the schema does NOT enforce that**, so the rule lives here and in the `COMMENT ON COLUMN` migration 0003 carries (PD-13). Executed: a photograph can name place P while naming a visit belonging to a different place, and the table accepts it. The paired CHECK a reader will reach for — `CHECK ((place_id IS NULL) = (visit_id IS NULL))`, the exact shape of `photos_coordinates_paired_ck` three columns away — is UNEXECUTABLE: it aborts D2's keep branch, because the two SET NULL rules fire as two separate single-column UPDATEs and the intermediate row is always incoherent. That is DEC-66's blocker recurring, and PD-13 carries the output. Ordinals are rewritten in `at` DESC, which is why visits.at is timestamptz and not date (DEC-68): the fixture visits Kyoto three times and a date column cannot break the tie.
5. PUT /v1/walks/{id} is setWalkName and dismissWalk. A dismissed walk is not a deleted walk — it keeps its points, and the read returns it.
6. **A BARE `Walk` MARSHALS `"points":null`** (CF-BLO-3, PD-15). `PUT /v1/walks/{id}` answers a Walk, and the client reads `(json['points'] as List<dynamic>)` with no null branch. `EmitWalk` lands here. **PHOTO NEEDS NONE AND THE REASON IS STATED**: `Photo` carries no list field, so `PUT /v1/photos/{id}` and `POST /v1/photos/{id}/refile` can answer a bare entity safely — measured, bare `Photo` carries no list key at all.
7. **THE POINTER CONTRACT ON THIS STEP'S FIVE ROUTES, AND IT IS WHERE IT MATTERS MOST** (DEC-89, SAF-MAJ-5, SAF-MAJ-6). Two of the three measured copies of the shipped defect are here. (a) A CAPTION-ONLY PUT MUST NOT UNFILE THE PHOTOGRAPH. Under the whole-state convention a body carrying only `{caption}` nulls `place_id` and `visit_id`, and the log has no record that the photograph was ever at Fushimi Inari — and it passes ALL THREE of this plan's standing guards, because the dangling check sees no dangling reference, the place-without-occasion query sees no place, and the pair-agreement assertion sees a pair that agrees. The client's own sentence about the half-state is 'a photograph naming a place but no occasion is half a record… and it is the half a count cannot see'; both halves gone is a state no count can see at all. (b) A `{dismissed:true}` OR `{name:"…"}` WALK PUT MUST NOT EMPTY THE TRACK. `walks_points_array_ck CHECK (jsonb_typeof(points) = 'array')` does not stop `points='[]'` because an empty array IS an array, and D2's sheet promises the walk survives BOTH branches — the only line on that sheet that is a promise rather than a choice. A `List<LatLng>` recorded on a day that has passed cannot be re-recorded. **WRITE EACH LEG TO SEND EXACTLY WHAT THE CONTROL SENDS**, not a synthesised whole entity: 'assert on what the widget actually renders' has a server twin, and it is 'assert against the body the client actually sends'.
8. **THE STANDING ASSERTION GAINS THE ONE IT COULD NOT MAKE** (DEC-89, SAF-MAJ-5). v7.1's 'after each of the five, `place_id IS NULL` and `visit_id IS NULL` AGREE' is the right constraint and is BLIND to the destruction it is positioned to catch — unfiling sets both to NULL, so the pair agrees and the assertion passes. Beside it now: **a COUNT THAT MUST NOT FALL.** `count(*) WHERE place_id IS NOT NULL` is unchanged across `PUT /v1/photos/{id}`, `POST /v1/photos/snooze`, `PUT /v1/walks/{id}` and `DELETE /v1/photos/{id}` where the photograph was unfiled, RISES on `refile`, and falls by a KNOWN amount on a delete of a filed photograph. The fixture's numbers make it writable and R4 measures them: 95 photographs carry both columns, 189 carry neither, place-only 0 and visit-only 0.
9. **`Walk.points` IS CAPPED AT 500 IN `ValidateWalk`, WITH ITS OWN 422 NAMING THE FIELD** (DEC-93, PD-21). The fixture's two walks carry SEVEN POINTS BETWEEN THEM, so every size argument in v7.0 and v7.1 was calibrated on a log with no real track in it. Marshalled through the shipped types: 1,000 points 51,004 B; 21,600 points 1,099,390 B — OVER the 1 MiB body ceiling, which is a six-hour walk at 1 Hz, so uncapped the user's LONGEST walk is the one write that silently cannot be saved. Enforce it in `ValidateWalk` and NOT by `http.MaxBytesReader`, which answers `ErrBodyTooLarge` with no field name. Migration 0003 carries the lower bound (`jsonb_array_length(points) > 0`) because DEC-89's contract makes `points: []` expressible. THE CLIENT'S OWN DECIMATION IS A CLIENT-PREREQUISITES ITEM: the server refusing an over-long track is not the same as the phone knowing to shorten one, and C2 draws a polyline that does not need every fix.
